papers.verdict_rationale: The complaint 'so much is very technical, users won't understand' is real but not evenly distributed. field-copy.ts and GraphView already prove the team knows how to fix this — every canonical enum got a plain-English question-and-answer treatment, and R9 (requirements-009.md) already recomposed the graph-review screen from 'honest everywhere and legible nowhere' into a checklist-first, one-alarm-per-card, consequence-behind-one-click layout. That pattern works and should not be discarded. The jargon problem is concentrated on three screens that never got the same treatment: the register list (raw enum values like 'pre_checked' render directly in the Stage column and filter chips), the verdict/sign-off page's 'WHY THIS VERDICT' block (a dense, unglossed run of rule IDs, citation brackets, and status chips), and the guided intake form (a parenthetical technical code appended to every one of ~90 options across 16 questions, read first by the non-technical 1LoD submitter). This is a scoped extension of an existing, working pattern to the screens that missed it — not a rethink of the information architecture or flow. A full redesign would throw away infrastructure (field-copy.ts, FIELD_CONSEQUENCES, the R9 checklist/disclosure components) that already does the job correctly where it was applied.
non_negotiables: Never delete an honesty disclosure to buy clarity — unsigned packs stay provisional, controls without evidence stay UNVERIFIED, the audit trail keeps saying it is client-side and proof-of-concept grade (CLAUDE.md, NF-2/NF-7). Aggregate, prioritise, or move behind one click (the R9 pattern) — never soften or cut, per requirements-009.md's own framing: 'Nothing honest is removed in this round — content becomes aggregated, prioritised, or one click away.'

The canonical technical vocabulary (enum values, rule IDs, control IDs) must stay retrievable on every screen that shows it today, because a risk or model-validation reader maps answers back to policy text against it — but it must never be the first or only thing a non-technical reader (1LoD submitter, or 2LoD scanning a list) sees.

No new label, chip, or sentence reaches a rendered screen without a plain-English companion. Extend field-copy.ts / FIELD_CONSEQUENCES / TIER_MEANINGS / TRACK_MEANINGS — do not hand-roll one-off copy that bypasses the one glossing source of truth.
Reserved-word discipline holds: no rendered string may match /approved|rejected/i outside the intended verdict language (CLAUDE.md gotcha) — any copy rewrite must re-check this before landing.

R9's proven disclosure shape (obligations-first checklist, meaning always visible, consequence one click away, one alarm per card) is the house style now. New work on the register list, verdict WHY section, and queue should reuse these components, not invent new disclosure patterns.
Determinism and evaluation logic stay untouched — every fix here is Rule 4 presentation-only (cross-cutting.md §7); nothing in src/components/* may inline business logic to achieve simpler copy.

findings.claim: The engine's internal stage enum renders verbatim as the Stage column value and as filter-chip labels, with no plain-English pass at all — the exact bug field-copy.ts was built to prevent, just not extended here.
findings.evidence: "Rows (18)... Approved with controls · Provisional | pre_checked | 23/08/2026" and "Filter chips: High · Medium · Low · Critical · Track II · Track I · pre_checked · approved · Approved with controls · Approved · Rejected" (03-register-list.txt); confirmed in evidence notes: "raw enum values render in Stage column ('pre_checked', 'approved') and filter chips."
findings.recommendation: Add a STAGE_LABELS map to field-copy.ts (e.g. pre_checked → 'Awaiting review', approved → 'Signed off') mirroring the existing DATA_CLASS_LABELS pattern, and use it for both the Stage column and the filter-chip text. Keep the raw enum as a data attribute/tooltip for anyone filtering by the technical value, never as the only label.

findings.claim: The status chip row stacks three overlapping vocabularies for one underlying message ('this is not final yet') — a business phrase, an honesty caveat, and a raw engine stage — forcing the reader to reconcile redundant signals instead of reading one message, which is exactly the defect Doumont names redundancy as.
findings.evidence: "[chips] Tier: High · Track: II · Approved with controls · Provisional · pre_checked" (04-register-detail-verdict.txt)
findings.recommendation: Collapse 'Approved with controls', 'Provisional', and 'pre_checked' into one lead status message ('Not final — 2 second-line reviews and 2LoD sign-off still needed') with the mechanism (which controls, which caveat, which stage) demoted to a secondary line or the existing 'What you need to do' block, which already does this well. Tier and Track stay as separate, genuinely distinct facts.

findings.claim: Every option across all 16 questions carries a parenthetical technical code, doubling the reading length of the exact screen the non-technical 1LoD submitter meets first — the code comment in field-copy.ts even says the parenthetical is 'kept... so a risk or model-validation reader can still map an answer back,' i.e. it is dead weight for the primary reader of this specific form.
findings.evidence: "Personal details of clients — names, accounts, anything identifying them (Client PII)" / "It substantially drives the decision a human then makes (material)" / "A neural network — e.g. image, voice or pattern recognition (deep learning)" — every one of ~90 options across the 16-question form (02-intake-guided-form.txt); field-copy.ts lines 22-24: "The technical term is kept in parentheses on each option so a risk or model-validation reader can still map an answer back to the vocabulary..."
findings.recommendation: Drop the parenthetical from the default rendered option text; render only the plain-language phrase. Add a per-question 'show technical terms' toggle (or a small info icon) that reveals the canonical vocabulary in a tooltip for the secondary reader — the same one-click-disclosure pattern R9 already applied to consequence lines on GraphView, applied here to the option codes instead.

findings.screen: Register → case detail (WHY THIS VERDICT section)
findings.claim: The rule list that explains the verdict is a dense, unbroken run of IDs and citation brackets with no structuring — the controls list two sections above gets a proven 'What it is / Why / What in place' three-line shape, but the invariant list that this verdict is actually reasoning from does not, so the reader's most important 'why' evidence is also its least scannable.
findings.evidence: "High: INV-AUTONOMY-02 …[OSFI E-23 §4.3; FCA Consumer Duty PRIN 2A]; INV-CONDUCT-01 …[RAF §4]; INV-DATA-01 …[GDPR Art. 32(1)(a)]; INV-DISCLOSE-01 …[EU AI Act Art. 50(1) — applies from 2026-08-02, NOT postponed by the Digital Omnibus]..." run on in one paragraph-like block (04-register-detail-verdict.txt), contrasted with the controls' "1. Bounded authority envelope + sampled post-hoc review CTRL-AUTONOMY-BOUND-01 [OUTSTANDING] / What it is: ... / Why this case needs it: ... / What 'in place' looks like: ..."
findings.recommendation: Apply the same three-line disclosure shape used for controls to each invariant: plain-English rule name, one-sentence firm-appetite reason (already present as the description), and citation demoted to a footnote marker rather than an inline bracketed string interrupting the sentence.

findings.screen: Register → case detail (multiple locations) and Rule-improvement queue
findings.claim: Internal requirement-tracking codes leak into sentences written for a bank reviewer, with no reader-facing purpose — Podmajersky's rule that a label is written for the reader who will act on it, not for the author's own traceability, is violated here.
findings.evidence: "Saved to register — awaiting active 2LoD sign-off (LC-2)." and "V1 is client-side — proof-of-concept grade for audit purposes (NF-2)." (04-register-detail-verdict.txt); "INV-AGENT-01 — 1 CHALLENGE · CHALLENGED 1 TIME · FIRED ON 1 DECIDED CASE" (06-about-and-queue-and-settings.txt)
findings.recommendation: Strip parenthetical spec/requirement IDs (LC-2, NF-2, R-numbers) from every rendered string; they belong in code comments and tests, which is where CLAUDE.md's citation discipline already lives for engine output. This loses no honesty content — the sentence's claim survives untouched with the ID removed. Also reword 'FIRED ON N DECIDED CASES' to plain language, e.g. 'has applied to N decided cases so far' — 'fired' is engine-trigger jargon in a sentence a risk reviewer reads.

findings.claim: Track and Tier render as bare chips in the list with zero inline meaning, even though the plain-English glosses already exist (TIER_MEANINGS, TRACK_MEANINGS) and are used one screen later — a reader scanning the list to decide what to open cannot decode the chip without opening a case first, which defeats the point of a scannable list (Redish: readers arrive to accomplish a task at the point where the eye lands, not after a click-through).
findings.evidence: "Columns: Use Case Name | Submitter | Tier | Track | Status..." with values like "High | II" and "Low | II" (03-register-list.txt) — no meaning shown; meanings only appear in TIER_MEANINGS/TRACK_MEANINGS (field-copy.ts) and are rendered on the detail page ("High tier means a lot could go wrong...", 04-register-detail-verdict.txt).
findings.recommendation: Wire the existing TIER_MEANINGS/TRACK_MEANINGS strings as a hover tooltip (or a small info affix) directly on the list-view Tier/Track chips. This is a wiring gap, not a copywriting gap — the strings already exist and are already approved.

findings.screen: Global header (every screen) and verdict detail folds
findings.claim: Several load-bearing governance terms get zero plain-English gloss anywhere in the captured evidence, unlike the fields that went through field-copy.ts — the product applies its own glossing discipline inconsistently.
findings.evidence: Header: "policy v1.3 · translation fidelity: unattested" (01-intake-describe.txt, present on every screen per sidebar note) — no expansion found in any captured screen. Verdict detail folds: "7 rules held by a single control · margin of safety 42% (your firm wants at least 10%)" and "The inherent position — the risk before any controls" / "the residual position — where the risk lands" (04-register-detail-verdict.txt) — 'inherent/residual', 'margin of safety', and 'translation fidelity' are used with no inline gloss comparable to what data_class or model_type received.
findings.recommendation: Extend the field-copy.ts pattern (plain phrase, technical term parenthetical or tooltip) to these terms — reuse the mechanism, don't invent new copy. A one-line tooltip on the header phrase ('nobody has yet confirmed the policy wording was correctly translated into these rules') and on 'margin of safety' would close this with no new component work.

findings.claim: A rule ID is the primary, lead label for each challenge entry, before any plain-language description — the reader has to already know the rulebook to identify what's being discussed at the point their eye first lands.
findings.evidence: "INV-AGENT-01 — 1 CHALLENGE · CHALLENGED 1 TIME · FIRED ON 1 DECIDED CASE — 'Internal-only reversible ticket routing at L3 feels over-weighted by this rule for technology operations tooling.'" (06-about-and-queue-and-settings.txt) — the rule ID leads; the human-readable challenge text trails it.
findings.recommendation: Lead with a short plain-language rule summary (already available from the invariant's description field used elsewhere in the app) with the ID as a trailing/secondary tag, matching the pattern already used for controls ('Bounded authority envelope + sampled post-hoc review CTRL-AUTONOMY-BOUND-01' — plain name first, ID second).

papers.proposed_direction: Do not redesign the information architecture or the flow — the six-step intake, graph-review, and sign-off sequence is sound, and the R9 recomposition of the graph-review screen (checklist-first, meaning-always-visible, consequence-one-click-away, one-alarm-per-card) already proves the team can solve exactly this complaint. The fix is to finish applying that same pattern and the same field-copy.ts glossing discipline to the three screens that never got it: the register list (map the stage enum to plain labels, surface Tier/Track meanings as tooltips), the verdict detail's WHY section (give invariants the same three-line What/Why/Citation structure controls already have, and collapse the redundant Approved-with-controls/Provisional/pre_checked chip stack into one lead status line), and the guided intake form (drop the parenthetical technical code from every option's default rendering and put it one click away, since the code comment itself admits it's there only for a secondary reader). Strip internal requirement-tracking IDs (LC-2, NF-2, R-numbers) out of user-facing sentences entirely — they add no reader value and were never meant to be there. None of this touches the engine, the audit trail, or any honesty disclosure; every change is presentation-only copy and disclosure-shape work, reusing components and copy tables that already exist and are already approved elsewhere in the product. Budget this as a handful of focused chunks (one per screen), not a ground-up visual redesign.

papers.panel: AI Governance (NIST AI RMF · Stuart Russell · Mitchell et al. Model Cards · OWASP LLM Top-10 · Christoph Molnar)
papers.verdict_rationale: The governance mechanics themselves are sound and mostly already hardened through five rounds of iteration (R5-R9): per-field AI-proposed/human-confirmed gating, quote-vs-guessed provenance, the no-plain-confirm-on-guessed-cards rule, the three-lever advisory/deciding split, and the honesty markers (UNVERIFIED, Provisional, translation fidelity: unattested) are all present and correctly wired. The 'too technical' complaint is real, but on inspection it clusters in specific, fixable spots — a raw YAML textarea presented as the primary policy view, raw internal enum values leaking into the register ('pre_checked'), and rule-ID-first phrasing crowding out the plain-English layer that already exists elsewhere (field-copy.ts, R9's checklist/one-alarm-per-card). These are presentation-layer fixes using a pattern this codebase has already proven works, not evidence the governance model itself needs to change. A full-redesign is the actual risk here: 'so much is very technical' is exactly the kind of complaint that invites deleting rule IDs, citations, provenance quotes, and the guessed/confirmed distinction in the name of friendliness — each of which is load-bearing for defensibility, not decoration. A bare patch under-responds: the raw-YAML exposure and the enum leakage recur across three separate screens (form, register, policy) and need a consistent presentation pass, not a one-line fix.
non_negotiables: Every AI-proposed field must stay visibly marked as proposed until a human confirms or corrects it — the guessed/quoted/no-basis-per-field distinction and the rule that a guessed card renders no plain 'confirm' button (ADR-IF-R6-2) are the entire mechanism preventing automation bias at intake and must survive any restyle untouched.

Model, vendor, and platform identity must remain explicit, correctable, first-class fields — never folded into a friendlier-but-vaguer question — because the firm's own invariants use exactly this data to detect an unapproved or silently-substituted model ('AI model versions must be pinned and outputs monitored for silent substitution').

The three-way distinction between firm appetite (decides), regulation (decides where it applies), and risk-knowledge (informs, never decides) must stay visually and structurally distinct everywhere it appears, with the advisory qualifier attached at the point of first mention — not only in a panel further down the page.

Hard lines, firm invariants, and jurisdiction-pack rules must remain three separately labeled categories with their own citation/provenance, never merged into one undifferentiated 'requirements' list — they carry different legal weight and different authorship and that difference is itself the governance content.

The attestation record (who confirmed, what was AI-proposed vs. human-corrected, provisional-until-signed-off status, 'Confirmed by you') must remain intact and visible; a simpler layout is not permitted to simplify away who attested to what.

No redesign may claim more certainty than the system has — UNVERIFIED control status, 'Provisional', 'translation fidelity: unattested' and similar honesty markers must survive verbatim; a friendlier tone is not license to round them off.

findings.claim: The verdict page carries three legally distinct rule categories — hard lines, firm invariants, jurisdiction-pack rules — each with different authorship and legal weight; a simplification pass aimed at 'less technical' is likely to collapse them into one undifferentiated list, erasing a distinction that matters for defensibility.
findings.evidence: "HARD LINES — NO CONTROL SET CAN FIX — Checked first. A use case crossing one is rejected immediately (PE-4)." versus "The inherent position — the risk before any controls. These are rules from your firm's risk appetite that this use case does not yet satisfy." versus "NO JURISDICTION RULEBOOK WAS APPLIED... no regulatory reasoning chain — no quoted source text, and none of the citations a pack would supply."
findings.recommendation: Keep the three-way taxonomy as a fixed structural element in any redesign — group and visually de-emphasize as needed, but never merge under one 'requirements' heading. Add a one-line legend once ('firm rule / law / hard limit') rather than removing the distinction to save space.

findings.claim: The per-field guessed/quoted/no-basis provenance markers and the rule that a guessed card gets no plain 'confirm' button are the only mechanism standing between an AI-proposed field and an unreviewed one — this reads as 'technical' UI clutter and is exactly what a naive simplification pass would strip first.
findings.evidence: "guessed — the description does not say. Correct it, or it becomes a question." and the code's own framing: "ADR-IF-R6-2: a guessed card renders NO plain confirm — cards with guessed fields are excluded from the unconfirmed set and resolve via correction or the questionnaire."
findings.recommendation: Non-negotiable — keep the gating logic exactly as is. If visual simplification is wanted, reduce badge chrome/styling weight (R9 already did this for the alarm banner), never the underlying rule. Explicitly reject any redesign proposal that offers a single 'confirm all' action capable of clearing a guessed field.

findings.claim: Model/vendor/platform identity fields read as jargon-heavy and business-unfriendly — the exact complaint driving this review — but they are the backbone of model-provenance and silent-substitution detection the firm's own invariants rely on; cutting them for friendliness would be a governance regression, not a simplification.
findings.evidence: field-copy.ts's own framing of the original complaint: "input data class, input data zone, AI model type... is not very business friendly, how will they know all this" (V2-E user feedback) — and the verdict's own invariant text: "AI model versions must be pinned and outputs monitored for silent substitution" (INV-TRACK2-01, cited on the sign-off page).
findings.recommendation: Keep the fields; the fix is presentation, already half-built — field-copy.ts's plain-English-with-parenthetical-technical-term pattern. Extend that pattern rather than removing 'which model/vendor/platform' from the form. Flag explicitly to the owner if any redesign proposal drops these fields.

findings.screen: Verdict / sign-off page (case detail, top of page)
findings.claim: The advisory risk-knowledge gap is surfaced at the very top of the page, ahead of the tier/track explanation, without its 'informs, never decides' qualifier attached at that point — under time pressure a 2LoD reviewer could read it as an outstanding requirement rather than advisory context, which is the risk-knowledge lever's whole design point to prevent.
findings.evidence: Top of page: "1 known risk class has no covering rule — see the risk-knowledge panel below." The actual disclaimer — "Informs — the rules decide. Nothing here changes the verdict for this case." — appears only much later, inside the separate "Risk-knowledge awareness" panel.
findings.recommendation: Attach a short inline qualifier to the top-line mention itself, e.g. "(advisory — not required for sign-off)", rather than relying on the reader to reach the panel below. Any redesign that makes this line more prominent must carry the qualifier with it, not strip it for brevity.

findings.claim: Raw internal enum values leak into the primary register UI untranslated — this is precisely the 'so much is very technical' experience the owner described, but it is engineering exhaust (a missing copy-map), not governance content, so it is a safe, no-loss simplification target rather than a reason to touch the underlying model.
findings.evidence: "Stage column (\"pre_checked\", \"approved\")" and "Filter chips: High · Medium · Low · Critical · Track II · Track I · pre_checked · approved · Approved with controls · Approved · Rejected" — raw enum tokens sitting next to already-translated tier/status labels in the same row.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same field-copy.ts plain-English pattern already used on the intake form and graph view to the register's Stage column and filter chips (e.g. 'pre_checked' → 'awaiting sign-off'). Zero governance information is lost by this translation.

findings.claim: Two columns ('Stale', 'Sampling') render blank for nearly all 18 rows, adding table width and visual noise without conveying governance information in their current column form.
findings.evidence: "Columns: Use Case Name | Submitter | Tier | Track | Status | Stage | Last Evaluated | Policy Version | Stale | Sampling" with only one row out of the sampled set carrying a value ('sampling review due'); the rest render empty.
findings.recommendation: Safe, non-governance simplification: replace the two mostly-empty columns with an inline badge shown only when the condition is true, rather than a column present in every row of any redesign.

findings.claim: The screen's primary artifact is a raw YAML textarea, which conflates two different needs — 'see and trust the rules that govern you' (essential transparency for both personas) and 'edit the rules as text' (a rule-authoring workflow the project's own docs say is deliberately human-led and out of band) — and is a likely major driver of the 'too technical' complaint.
findings.evidence: "Policy YAML [large textarea of the raw YAML file] [Validate] [Save]" positioned directly below the three lever cards ("Firm appetite — Decides. | Regulation — Decides, where the law applies. | Risk knowledge — Informs — never decides.") and the hard-lines list.
findings.recommendation: Keep the lever cards, hard-lines list, and jurisdiction-pack sign-off status as the primary, human-readable view (non-negotiable, essential transparency). Move raw YAML editing behind an explicit 'Edit as YAML' affordance for the rule-authoring workflow, so the default screen a submitter or reviewer lands on is not a code editor.

findings.claim: The tool's own self-assessment case is listed as an ordinary register row, distinguished from real business use cases only by a column value, risking a rushed reviewer treating a circular self-assessment as an ordinary case.
findings.evidence: "AIGate (self-assessment) | system | Medium | II | Approved with controls · Provisional | pre_checked | 23/08/2026 | 1.3" — rendered in the same row format as "Retail banking assistant chatbot | 2LoD | High | II ..." with only the Submitter cell ('system') differing.
findings.recommendation: Give the self-assessment row distinct visual treatment (not just a column value) in any redesign, consistent with the page-level banner that already separately calls it out ('AIGate self-assessment pending 2LoD approval...').

papers.proposed_direction: Keep the engine, the gating logic (NODE_CONFIRMED, guessed-card no-confirm, provenance quotes), and the three-lever advisory/deciding architecture completely untouched — none of the owner's complaint traces to these being wrong, and Russell's corrigibility principle and Mitchell et al.'s 'documentation travels with the model' both argue for keeping them exactly as strict as they are. Do a presentation-layer pass, reusing the pattern that already worked in field-copy.ts and R9's checklist/one-alarm-per-card redesign of the graph screen: translate every remaining raw enum or internal stage code the register and policy screens still leak (AIG-5, AIG-6), move raw YAML editing behind an explicit advanced affordance so the policy screen's default view is the human-readable lever cards and jurisdiction table (AIG-7), and attach the advisory qualifier to the risk-knowledge gap line at its first mention on the verdict page, not only in the panel below (AIG-4). Treat rule/control IDs (INV-AUTONOMY-01, CTRL-ENC-01) as secondary-weight text next to the plain-English label they already have, rather than removing them — a 2LoD reviewer needs the exact ID for audit citation even if a 1LoD submitter does not read it. Before any visual-density work on the verdict page proceeds, restate the hard-line/invariant/jurisdiction-pack trichotomy as an explicit constraint in the redesign brief, since it is the single distinction most likely to be silently lost under 'make it feel less technical' pressure. The end state should be a UI that looks less technical because the technical content is better organized and better translated — not because any of it was removed.

papers.panel: Regulation & supervisory defensibility (PRA SS1/23, SR 26-2, EU AI Act, OSFI E-23, MAS FEAT, Michael Power)
papers.verdict_rationale: The underlying disclosure architecture is sound and, on the one screen it has already been applied to (graph review, via requirements-009 / R9), proves that density can be fixed by aggregation, prioritisation and one-click deferral without deleting any honesty content. That pattern needs to be extended to the other screens a 2LoD reviewer or a supervisor actually stops on — the verdict/sign-off page, the register list, and the policy screen — none of which have had an R9-equivalent pass yet. A full redesign risks re-deriving these disclosures from scratch and losing the specific caveats (unverified identity, provisional qualifiers, "restates the record; does not strengthen it") that are exactly what a supervisor doing effective-challenge review would look for, and that Michael Power's critique says are the first casualties of a "make it less scary" pass. A patch is insufficient because the density problem is structural on at least three more screens, not a single cosmetic tweak.
non_negotiables: Every rule application keeps its exact regulatory citation (statute/article/section — SS1/23 §3.4, EU AI Act Art 50(1), GDPR Art 32(1)(a), OSFI E-23 §4.3, etc.) visibly attached to the verdict line it supports; citations may be reflowed or grouped but never summarised away.

Provisional / UNVERIFIED / OUTSTANDING status must stay visually inseparable from the verdict or control it qualifies — 'Approved with controls' must never render, scroll, or export without its 'Provisional' qualifier in the same visual unit (NF-7's honesty requirement; SS1/23 and MAS FEAT would both read a dropped qualifier as overclaiming model state).

The audit trail stays append-only, complete, and openly labelled proof-of-concept/client-side grade (NF-2) — it is the one artifact a supervisor will ask to inspect directly, so no redesign may filter, collapse, or silently paginate it out of default view.

Named human sign-off (2LoD reviewer name + timestamp) stays a distinct, deliberate action separate from any automated recommendation, and its 'self-asserted, not verified' caveat stays adjacent to the Approve control, not demoted into a tooltip — this is the effective-challenge moment SS1/23 is built around, and hiding its weakest link makes the sign-off look stronger than it is.

The three-lever separation — firm appetite decides, regulation decides where it applies, risk knowledge only informs — stays visually distinct on every screen it appears; MAS FEAT's accountability principle requires the actual decision-maker to be traceable, and blending an advisory taxonomy match into decision-styled content would misrepresent an advisory input as authoritative.

The rule → control → citation → evidence-status chain (the minimal-fix set) stays traceable end to end; this chain is literally what SS1/23-style effective challenge is checking for, and collapsing it into a generic checklist breaks the one thing a supervisor can verify against the underlying rulebook.

findings.claim: The page's genuinely defensibility-critical content (binding constraint, citations, outstanding-control count, jurisdiction status) is real and correctly rendered, but competes with so much structurally-identical content that a reviewer can plausibly click Approve without having processed it — the exact 'checking becomes ritual' failure Michael Power describes, where attestation stops binding to the thing it is supposed to attest to.
findings.evidence: requirements-009.md: "'honest everywhere and legible nowhere.' Each disclosure... is individually correct; their sum is ~1,200–1,600px for a three-card case, with the constant... visually indistinguishable from the variable... up to three same-styled alarms per card, required actions scattered across columns." This diagnosis was written about the graph-review screen and fixed there by R9; the verdict/sign-off page (evidence file 04) shows the same shape unaddressed: a long undifferentiated run from the VERDICT block through 12 triggered invariants with citations before any fold appears.
findings.recommendation: Apply R9's own pattern to this screen: a short state-derived checklist at the top of the sign-off page — binding constraint name, jurisdiction-pack status, outstanding-control count, sign-off gate — each item scrolling to its section, mirroring R9-SC-1 exactly. Keep the already-collapsed folds (fragility, platform inheritance, living status) as-is; they are the right instinct, just not yet extended upward to the page's opening block.

findings.screen: Register detail / verdict sign-off page — attestation block
findings.claim: The self-asserted-identity caveat is the ugliest, least 'finished-looking' string on the sign-off page and therefore the single piece of text most likely to be cut or shrunk by a redesign aimed at looking less technical — but it is exactly the caveat a supervisor doing SS1/23 effective-challenge review needs to see at the point of signing, not buried in help text.
findings.evidence: 04-register-detail-verdict.txt: "Your name [input] — Recorded on the attestation so the trail says who accepted this verdict. It is self-asserted — this build has no sign-in, so the name is not verified."
findings.recommendation: Treat this line as protected, not as clutter: keep it directly beside the name field and the Approve button, full weight, in any restyle. If the redesign compresses help text generally, this specific caveat should be the one exception carved out explicitly, with a one-line note in the design brief saying why.

findings.claim: The memo's self-limiting caption is a deliberate guard against the memo being read as independent challenge when it is generated from the same record it is supposed to challenge — precisely the audit-theatre pattern Power warns about — and is at high risk of being trimmed as an unnecessary hedge during a simplification pass, since a non-expert editor has no reason to know why it matters.
findings.evidence: 04-register-detail-verdict.txt: "[button] Download effective-challenge memo (markdown) — A 2LoD-style memo generated from this record. It restates the record; it does not strengthen it."
findings.recommendation: Keep the full caption verbatim under any redesign; if button copy is being shortened generally, exempt this one and, if anything, place 'restates the record; does not strengthen it' even closer to the button rather than in secondary text, since it is the only thing preventing the memo being mistaken for independent validation.

findings.claim: The register-level provisional rollup — the single sentence a supervisor reviewing the whole book (not one case) would want first — is styled as ordinary body text competing with an 11-chip filter row that itself leaks raw enum values, diluting the one line that matters most at register scope.
findings.evidence: 03-register-list.txt: "AIGate self-assessment pending 2LoD approval — verdicts are provisional until cleared." / "4 of 18 verdicts here would be final once outstanding sign-offs land." ... "Filter chips: High · Medium · Low · Critical · Track II · Track I · pre_checked · approved · Approved with controls · Approved · Rejected" ... "NOTE: raw enum values render in Stage column (\"pre_checked\", \"approved\") and filter chips."
findings.recommendation: Give the provisional rollup its own banner/card, visually separated from the filter-chip row — the register-list equivalent of R9-SC-1's checklist header. Route the Stage column and its filter chips through the same label-mapping approach field-copy.ts already applies to guided-form copy, so 'pre_checked' never reaches a reviewer's screen as raw enum text.

findings.screen: Guided intake form / graph review — decision_type and hitl fields
findings.claim: Two decision-bearing fields whose absence changes the regulatory analysis can be left blank by design, and blank renders identically to any other 'not stated' field with no additional visual flag distinguishing 'submitter deliberately left this blank' from an unremarkable unanswered optional field — so a reviewer has no signal to go check whether the omission was considered.
findings.evidence: 02-intake-guided-form.txt: "Leave blank only if it feeds no decision at all." field-copy.ts: decision_type consequence — "Names the decision the rulebook must cover. Credit and lending decisions carry the highest floors." GraphView.tsx: `const meaning = has ? spec.meanings?.[String(raw)] ?? String(raw) : 'not stated';` — the guessed-badge/no-basis styling in the same block is driven by `quotes`/`guessed`, which default to `{}` on the guided-form path, so a blank decision-bearing field on that path gets no comparable flag.
findings.recommendation: Give an unanswered decision-bearing field (decision_type, hitl) the same visual weight as a guessed field when it renders as 'not stated' — a quiet badge equivalent to the existing guessed-badge, not a new alarm — so the reviewer sees that a materially relevant field was left silent, not just that it happens to say 'not stated' like any other optional value.

findings.claim: Raw YAML editing and reviewer-facing governance content (jurisdiction sign-off status, hard lines) sit on the same page with no separation by audience, so a submitter or 2LoD reviewer checking 'what rule fired and is the relevant jurisdiction pack signed off' has to scroll past — and risks editing — a raw source-of-truth file that CLAUDE.md itself says should only ever be touched by whoever authors packs.
findings.evidence: 05-policy-screen.txt: "Policy YAML [large textarea of the raw YAML file] [Validate] [Save]" immediately precedes "JURISDICTION PACKS ... UK United Kingdom — 1 rule applying — not yet signed off". CLAUDE.md: "Rule/pack authoring — human-led, never generated" is called out as a distinct concern from general product use.
findings.recommendation: Split the shared 'what rule applies, what's signed off' view (what a supervisor or reviewer consults) from the raw-YAML editor (what a pack author uses) — same underlying data, two entry points, so the citation/status view a non-technical reader lands on isn't gated behind a screenful of YAML.

findings.claim: A human-filed dissent and a system-filed coverage-gap entry are attributed with the same visual treatment, which risks a supervisor reading a template-generated 'gap' entry as a human 2LoD judgment call — understating how much of the queue's volume is actually manual challenge versus automated flagging.
findings.evidence: 06-about-and-queue-and-settings.txt: "Marcus Chen (seeded sample) (name not verified) · on [IB] Technology — Incident-ticket triage agent" and, styled identically, "2LoD (risk-knowledge lens, MIT AI Risk Repository…) (name not verified) · on Retail banking assistant chatbot".
findings.recommendation: Add a small source tag distinguishing 'filed by a human reviewer' from 'filed automatically from a risk-knowledge coverage gap' so anyone auditing the queue for actual dissent volume isn't misled by mixed provenance under uniform styling.

findings.claim: The advisory-never-decides framing for the MIT AI Risk Repository panel is correctly and prominently stated, and should be explicitly protected — this is the one place on the page where an external, non-firm, non-regulatory source could most easily be mistaken for a decision input if a redesign blends its visual treatment with the invariant/citation list above it.
findings.evidence: 04-register-detail-verdict.txt: "What a recognized external risk taxonomy says this shape of use case is known to risk. Informs — the rules decide. Nothing here changes the verdict for this case."
findings.recommendation: Keep this panel visually distinct (different container, not just a different heading) from the WHY THIS VERDICT invariant list in any restyle, so the appetite/regulation/knowledge lever distinction survives a density pass even if the panel itself is compacted or collapsed by default.

papers.proposed_direction: Extend the R9 pattern — aggregate, prioritise, or defer one click away, never delete — to every screen a 2LoD reviewer or supervisor actually stops on, not just the graph-review screen it was built for. The sign-off page needs an R9-SC-1-style checklist at the top (binding constraint, jurisdiction status, outstanding-control count, sign-off gate) while its existing folds stay closed by default; the register list needs its provisional rollup promoted to its own banner and its raw enum leakage routed through the same label maps field-copy.ts already uses; the policy screen needs its raw-YAML editor separated from the citation/status view a non-author actually consults. Every citation chip, VERIFIED/UNVERIFIED tag, provisional qualifier, and append-only audit disclosure named above stays exactly as it is in content — only position, grouping, and default visibility change. The caveats that currently read as hedges — unverified reviewer identity, "restates the record; does not strengthen it", proof-of-concept-grade audit trail — are the parts most likely to be trimmed by an editor optimising for "looks less scary", and they are precisely the content SS1/23 effective-challenge review and Power's audit-society critique are watching for; removing them to make the tool feel more finished would be the one change that actually damages defensibility while everything else here is purely presentational.

papers.panel: Banking practice & the two users (SR 11-7 effective challenge; Emanuel Derman, Models.Behaving.Badly; Cathy O'Neil, Weapons of Math Destruction) — role-played through James (1LoD developer, 10 minutes) and Priya (2LoD AI-risk reviewer, queue of 12)
papers.verdict_rationale: Walking both personas end to end, the product's hard-won structure is sound and should not be rebuilt: a deterministic engine, every verdict traced to a named rule and citation, honesty markers (provisional, UNVERIFIED, guessed) that are exactly the anti-Derman, anti-O'Neil posture this product needs, and a three-lever ownership model (firm decides / regulation decides / knowledge informs) that is unusually legible for a risk product. R9 already proved the fix pattern that works here — aggregate, prioritise, or move behind one click, never delete a disclosure — and did it successfully for the single worst screen (graph review). The owner's "too confusing" complaint traces to concrete, nameable defects: raw enum leakage on the register (undoing the plain-language work done everywhere else), one page serving both James's action list and Priya's full effective-challenge dossier with no role-aware default state or gating on sign-off actions, jargon still riding inline in every form option label, and a register with no "what's mine to act on" view for a reviewer with 12 live cases. None of these require re-architecting the graph model, the rule-trace concept, or the control/evidence apparatus — they require applying the R9 pattern (state-derived checklist, collapse-by-default, one-click reveal, role-aware defaults) to two more screens plus a copy-layer consistency pass. That is a targeted redesign, not a rebuild from the whiteboard.
non_negotiables: Every verdict stays traceable to a named rule and citation even when compressed for James — collapsing content for one audience must never mean deleting the evidence trail Priya needs to sign off defensibly (the R9-NF-1 precedent: aggregate or one-click-away, never delete).

Provisional / UNVERIFIED / guessed / no-verified-basis honesty markers keep their current strength — CLAUDE.md's 'honesty is a functional requirement' and SR 11-7 effective challenge both depend on the reviewer never being told more than the system can prove. No softening these to make the redesign feel friendlier.

The three-lever ownership model (Firm appetite decides / Regulation decides where it applies / Risk knowledge only informs) stays explicit and visible on every rule-bearing screen — this is the product's clearest working answer to Cathy O'Neil's opacity critique of algorithmic scoring, and the fastest way a first-time reviewer builds trust in the tool.

Sign-off actions (Approve / Request correction / Challenge a rule) must never become reachable, or visually indistinguishable from informational content, for a role not authorised to take them — role-aware defaults may reorder or collapse, but must not blur who is accountable for clicking what.

Plain-language simplification is strictly a rendering concern (field-copy.ts and its siblings) — it must never reduce the underlying question set, field coverage, or citation depth that feeds the deterministic engine or the audit trail.

findings.claim: The single verdict page renders James's short action summary and Priya's full effective-challenge dossier -- including the sign-off action controls -- back to back with no role-aware default state or gating, so a 1LoD submitter and a 2LoD reviewer see (and can click) the same page.
findings.evidence: "What you need to do / Put 9 controls in place, and 2 separate reviews that other teams own still apply. Then a second-line reviewer signs off." is followed, after 18 invariants with citation chips, two folds, a risk-knowledge panel and a similar-cases panel, by: "Your name [input] ... Notes (optional) [textarea]   [Approve] [Request correction] [Challenge a rule...]" with nothing on the page distinguishing which role should be looking at which block.
findings.recommendation: Default-collapse everything from "WHY THIS VERDICT" through "similar decided cases" behind a single "Full reasoning & sign-off (2LoD)" expander; keep "What you need to do" as James's whole screen. Render the Approve/Request correction/Challenge block only when the active role is 2LoD -- not merely present-but-ignorable.

findings.claim: Raw engine enum values leak straight into the register table and its filter chips, undoing the plain-language rewrite the rest of the product (field-copy.ts) was explicitly built to do.
findings.evidence: "raw enum values render in Stage column (\"pre_checked\", \"approved\") and filter chips" -- confirmed against the rendered columns "Stage" showing pre_checked / approved and the filter-chip row listing the same tokens alongside human labels like "Approved with controls".
findings.recommendation: Route Stage values and filter-chip labels through a label map in the same spirit as TIER_MEANINGS/TRACK_MEANINGS already in field-copy.ts -- "pre_checked" -> "Pre-checked, awaiting sign-off", "approved" -> "Approved". This is a one-file consistency fix, not new design.

findings.claim: Every option across the form's nine-plus select fields still carries the raw technical enum inline in the primary, clickable label -- the plain-English rewrite (field-copy.ts) wraps the jargon rather than removing it from James's first read.
findings.evidence: "Personal details of clients -- names, accounts, anything identifying them (Client PII)" / "A chatbot or writing assistant -- understands and produces text (LLM)" / "A model trained on historical data -- general machine learning (ML)" -- the parenthetical technical term appears on literally every option button.
findings.recommendation: Demote the parenthetical enum to a small muted suffix or a hover tooltip rather than inline in the clickable label text. field-copy.ts's own comment says the term is kept for "a risk or model-validation reader" -- so keep it reachable, just not load-bearing for a first-time business reader's scan.

findings.claim: Priya, with 12 live cases, has no default view of "what's mine to act on" -- she lands on a flat 18-row table and must self-assemble the right filter chips every session.
findings.evidence: "4 of 18 verdicts here would be final once outstanding sign-offs land." sits above an undifferentiated filter-chip row: "High · Medium · Low · Critical · Track II · Track I · pre_checked · approved · Approved with controls · Approved · Rejected" with no "awaiting my sign-off" default or saved view.
findings.recommendation: Default the register landing state to stage=pre_checked AND tier requiring 2LoD sign-off (exactly the count the summary line already computes), with the full unfiltered table one click away. This turns an existing number into a working default, not a new feature.

findings.claim: Field help text mixes a plain business question with a full risk-methodology paragraph that is permanently visible, at a density inconsistent with a stated ten-minute budget.
findings.evidence: "Not where the data is stored -- where it gets sent to be processed. A cloud AI service counts as an outside supplier even if your data normally never leaves the firm. Information moving from a more protected place to a less protected one is the single thing these rules watch for most closely."
findings.recommendation: Apply the same one-click disclosure pattern already built and approved for consequence lines (requirements-009.md R9-SC-2: meaning always visible, consequence behind one click) to form help text -- a one-line plain prompt by default, "why we ask" expandable on demand.

findings.claim: The sidebar item James would open to answer "can I build this at all" ("§ Appetite framework") leads to a raw-YAML editor with Validate/Save controls, with no visible role qualifier on the nav item -- unlike the adjacent "⚑ Rule challenges (2LoD only)" item, which is explicitly gated.
findings.evidence: Sidebar: "+ New pre-check · ▤ Register (count) · § Appetite framework · ⚑ Rule challenges (2LoD only) · ? About"; policy screen: "Policy YAML [large textarea of the raw YAML file] [Validate] [Save]".
findings.recommendation: Split the page: keep the plain-English lever cards and hard-line list open to both roles as useful pre-submission context; gate the raw-YAML edit/save control behind 2LoD the same way rule challenges already are, so a 1LoD developer can read but never touch firm appetite.

findings.claim: On the fast path James is most likely to prefer (describe in plain English rather than fill 16 fields), the graph-review screen reintroduces the time cost the fast path was meant to save: up to three mutually exclusive per-field badge states plus an optional consequence line plus an optional plausibility warning, repeated per field, per node.
findings.evidence: Per field: "based on: “...”" or "guessed -- the description does not say. Correct it, or it becomes a question." or "model confident -- no verified basis" (GraphView.tsx NodeCard render, three branches per FieldSpec), plus a per-card uncertainty banner ("The model was not confident about this part") and a per-card "Why these values matter" toggle.
findings.recommendation: Extend the R9-SC-1 checklist pattern one step further: collapse fully-confident, quoted fields into a one-line “N fields confirmed automatically” summary per card by default, auto-expanding only guessed or uncertain fields. Nothing is deleted (satisfies R9-NF-1) -- it changes what is expanded by default on a clean extraction, cutting James's read surface roughly in half.

papers.proposed_direction: Keep the engine, the rule-trace model, the three-lever framing, and every existing honesty marker exactly as they are — none of that is what is confusing anyone. Apply the R9 pattern (state-derived checklist header, collapse-by-default, reveal-on-demand, nothing deleted) to the two screens that never got it: the register list and the verdict/sign-off page. Make role the organizing default rather than an afterthought — Priya's register opens on "awaiting my sign-off"; James's verdict page opens on "what you need to do" with everything else, including the sign-off controls, behind a clearly labeled 2LoD expander. Close the plain-language gaps that survived the earlier rewrite: raw enum values in the register's Stage column and filter chips, and the inline technical parentheticals on every guided-form option, both fixable through the label-map pattern field-copy.ts already established. Gate the raw-YAML policy editor behind 2LoD the same way rule challenges already are, since it currently sits one click from a 1LoD developer just looking for context. On the LLM intake path, extend the checklist idea to the field level so a clean, confident extraction reads as a short confirmation rather than a wall of badges. None of this touches the engine, the citation trail, or the control/evidence apparatus Priya's SR 11-7 defensibility depends on — it is copy, defaults, and role-awareness layered onto a structure that is already doing the hard part correctly.

papers.verdict_rationale: The domain complexity is real and mostly earned — R9 already proved the right move is aggregation/prioritization, not deletion, and that pattern should be extended, not abandoned. But three structural problems recur across almost every screen and won't be fixed by more copy patches: (1) internal requirement/ADR IDs (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4) and raw enum values (pre_checked, approved) are rendered directly as end-user prose — this is the system's internal structure leaking straight through the UI, the textbook Cooper violation; (2) the 16-question guided form is the engine's canonical vocabulary wearing a costume — the team's own code comment admits the earlier version "exposed the engine's internal field names as labels" and the fix was "presentation-only," which is exactly the kind of patch Krug warns produces a form that still needs a help paragraph under nearly every question; (3) one verdict page serves two personas with opposite goals (1LoD "what do I do", 2LoD "is this defensible") with the same scroll order, burying the sign-off action beneath several panels of reasoning every time. None of this requires rebuilding the engine, the audit model, or the honesty disclosures — it requires reordering, relabeling, and removing IDs that never should have been user-facing, which is a targeted redesign, not a full one.
non_negotiables: Never delete a disclosure to make a screen feel simpler — R9 already established the correct move is aggregate, prioritise, or put one click away, never remove; any redesign must extend that precedent, not reverse it.

The deterministic, non-chatbot framing and the plain-English 'why' behind a verdict must stay visible — simplifying for Krug's trunk test must not slide into hiding the reasoning a 2LoD reviewer needs to defend a decision (that's the product's whole value proposition).

Every screen leads with the persona's actual question before its supporting mechanism — 1LoD gets 'what do I need to do' first, 2LoD gets the action bar within reach without scrolling past the full rules audit every time.

No internal spec/requirement/ADR identifiers (INV-*, CTRL-*, HL-*, PE-4, NF-2, LC-2, VD-4, the bare word 'invariant') appear in rendered end-user copy — they belong in code comments and test selectors, never in prose a submitter or reviewer reads.
Any rewritten copy still avoids the reserved words flagged in CLAUDE.md ('approved'/'rejected' as bare strings break the verdict-screen test query) — redesign must not reintroduce a known regression.

Restructuring the guided form changes presentation only — the canonical vocabulary and field names the engine scores on (policy-schema.md §3.0) are untouched; this is a UI flow change, not a data-model change.

findings.claim: Internal requirement/ADR IDs are rendered as parenthetical citations inside ordinary end-user prose, with no gloss — pure system-structure leakage into the task surface.
findings.evidence: "Saved to register — awaiting active 2LoD sign-off (LC-2)." / "Audit trail is append-only. V1 is client-side — proof-of-concept grade for audit purposes (NF-2)." / "HARD LINES — NO CONTROL SET CAN FIX — Checked first. A use case crossing one is rejected immediately (PE-4)."
findings.recommendation: Strip these parenthetical spec-ID citations from every rendered string. If traceability to the requirement is valuable for an internal audit, carry it as a title attribute, a data attribute, or a footnote reference table — never inline in a sentence a business user or 2LoD reviewer reads as the explanation itself. This is Krug's trunk test failing at the exact moment a user is trying to understand what just happened to their case.

findings.claim: Raw internal enum/state-machine values render directly in a column and in filter chips a 2LoD reviewer scans daily.
findings.evidence: "NOTE: raw enum values render in Stage column (\"pre_checked\", \"approved\") and filter chips." and the column list itself: "Tier | Track | Status | Stage | Last Evaluated | Policy Version | Stale | Sampling" where Status already reads "Approved with controls · Provisional" alongside a separate Stage of "pre_checked".
findings.recommendation: Apply the same labels-dictionary discipline the codebase already uses in field-copy.ts to the Stage column and filter chips. Separately, question whether Stage needs to exist as a distinct column from Status at all — right now a reviewer sees two overlapping classification systems (one human-legible, one internal) side by side with no explanation of how they differ.

findings.claim: The 16-field (13 required) form is the engine's canonical vocabulary with plain-language labels bolted on, not a goal-directed conversation — and the team's own commit history shows this was already tried as a copy-only fix once and the underlying structure was left alone.
findings.evidence: field-copy.ts's own comment: "The form previously exposed the engine's internal field names as labels and its raw enum values as options... So the fix is presentation-only: the values stay, the words the user reads become questions..." — and nearly every select in the rendered form ships with a help paragraph ("Pick the most sensitive kind it touches, even if that's only occasionally", "Not where the data is stored — where it gets sent to be processed..."), which is Krug's own diagnostic: a control that needs a paragraph of help next to it usually needs redesigning, not explaining.
findings.recommendation: Group the 16 fields into 3-4 goal-oriented sections a submitter already thinks in (what it is / what it touches / what it can do / who sees it), progressively disclose the three optional fields (platform, vendor, decision type — currently same visual weight as the 13 required ones) behind an 'advanced' toggle, and make the plain-language description path the default entry point rather than something unlocked only after visiting Settings to point at a local model — Cooper's persona-goal principle says the majority who 'just want to describe what they built' shouldn't default into the compliance taxonomy.

findings.claim: The same page layout serves both personas' opposite goals in one fixed scroll order, and the actual task action (sign-off) sits at the very bottom, beneath a full rules audit, two closed-by-default folds, a jurisdiction note, a control-evidence table, a risk-knowledge panel, and a similar-cases panel.
findings.evidence: Rendered order per the capture: Provisional banner → VERDICT → "What you need to do" → "WHY THIS VERDICT" ("Evaluated against 5 hard lines and 18 invariants — 12 triggered") → fragility fold → platform-inheritance fold → jurisdiction note → control-evidence table → risk-knowledge panel → similar-cases panel → only then "Your name [input]... [Approve] [Request correction] [Challenge a rule…]".
findings.recommendation: Pin the sign-off action bar (name, notes, Approve/Request correction/Challenge) directly under the verdict summary as a sticky element, with an in-page 'read the full reasoning' jump link for the 2LoD reviewer who wants to verify before signing. Fogg's behavior model: the trigger for the wanted action must land while motivation is high, not after a long scroll of caveats that can talk a reviewer out of finishing.

findings.claim: Field labels on the review card regress to raw taxonomy terms the guided-form question never used, so a submitter doesn't recognize their own answer.
findings.evidence: The guided form asks "How much weight does its output carry?" and "If it gets something wrong, can it be undone?" — but GraphView.tsx's OUTPUT_FIELDS render the same values under bare labels: `{ field: 'decision_bindingness', label: 'decision bindingness', ... }` and `{ field: 'output_reversibility', label: 'output reversibility', ... }`.
findings.recommendation: Reuse the question phrasing (or a short derivative of it) as the `dt` label on the review card instead of the underscored engine field name with spaces substituted in, so the review screen speaks the same language the intake question did.

findings.claim: A third, unexplained confidence category — 'model confident — no verified basis' — sits beside 'based on: quote' and the 'guessed' badge, adding a distinction a non-technical submitter has no use for and no action to take on.
findings.evidence: `model confident — no verified basis` rendered whenever a field has no quote, isn't guessed, and the card isn't marked uncertain.
findings.recommendation: For the 1LoD persona this reads as an alarm attached to nothing actionable — there is no button beside it, unlike the guessed badge's 'Fix guessed values' affordance. Either fold it into the existing 'guessed' visual language or reword it to something task-oriented ('worth a second look — not found in your text') rather than surfacing the internal provenance-validation state as its own category.

findings.claim: An unexplained technical status renders in the header on every screen a first-time user sees, before any content.
findings.evidence: "AIGate PRE-CHECK ENGINE · policy v1.3 · translation fidelity: unattested" — present in the header on the very first intake screen.
findings.recommendation: This fails Krug's trunk test at the top of literally every page. Either move the phrase to About/Settings where it can be explained once, or compress it to a small labeled chip with a tooltip — the same pattern the product already uses well for pack 'pending adoption' chips.

findings.claim: A compact stat line uses the bare engineering term 'invariants' two lines above the product's own plain-English gloss of the same word — the glossary discipline exists but isn't reused everywhere.
findings.evidence: "Evaluated against 5 hard lines and 18 invariants — 12 triggered." immediately followed a few lines later by "Invariants are your firm's risk appetite rules; each one names the controls that satisfy it..."
findings.recommendation: Reuse the existing gloss in the stat line itself: '5 hard lines and 18 firm rules.' Small fix, but this exact kind of drift — a careful translation written once and not propagated — is how jargon quietly reaccumulates in a product that has otherwise invested real effort in plain language.

papers.proposed_direction: Keep the engine, the audit trail, and every honesty disclosure exactly as they are — none of this is a data-model or determinism problem, and R9 already proved the right lever is aggregation, not deletion. Do a single systematic sweep removing every internal identifier (spec IDs, ADR references, raw enum/state values) from rendered copy, the same discipline field-copy.ts already applies to the engine's canonical vocabulary but hasn't been applied to the requirements-tracking layer or the register's stage machine. Split the verdict page's fixed scroll order by persona intent: pin the sign-off action bar near the top for the 2LoD reviewer instead of after five panels of evidence, and keep "what you need to do" as the first thing a 1LoD submitter sees, exactly as it already mostly is. Restructure the 16-question guided form from a flat enumeration of engine fields into 3-4 grouped, goal-oriented sections with the three optional fields behind progressive disclosure, and make the plain-language description path the default rather than something gated behind a Settings visit — per Cooper, the form should follow the submitter's mental model of describing what they built, not the policy schema's mental model of what it needs to score it. Carry the field-copy.ts vocabulary-mapping discipline through to the graph-review card labels so a submitter recognizes their own answer restated in the same words they used to give it, and fix the two or three spots (masthead, invariant stat line, provenance badge) where a plain-English translation exists elsewhere in the product but wasn't reused. None of this is a rebuild; it's finishing the translation work the team already started and proved works with R9.

papers.panel: Information layout & accessibility (Few, Tufte, WCAG 2.1, Pickering)
papers.verdict_rationale: The content and honesty model are sound, and the codebase already contains a proven fix for this exact defect class: requirements-009.md documents a prior design review that found the graph-review screen "honest everywhere and legible nowhere" and fixed it with a specific, now-validated pattern (state-derived checklist, consequences behind one click, one alarm per card, folds ordered by importance). That pattern was applied to GraphView.tsx only. The same disease is visible, unfixed, on the verdict/sign-off screen and the register list — a fully-expanded 12-rule citation block sits above three folded panels of lesser weight, the Provisional banner is not the first thing read, raw enum values ('pre_checked') leak into the register table that field-copy.ts exists specifically to prevent elsewhere, and the guided form's 16 questions run as one flat list despite the underlying model already having the three-part Input/Processing/Output structure GraphView renders. None of this requires new visual language, new copy voice, or new information — it requires applying the R9 pattern consistently instead of once. That is a targeted-redesign: real restructuring on 2-3 screens, not a one-line patch, but not a rebuild of a design system that already works where it was applied.
non_negotiables: Every honesty marker (PROVISIONAL, UNVERIFIED, OUTSTANDING, guessed, no-verified-basis) stays legible via text or icon, never color alone (WCAG 1.4.1) — the current build already does this correctly and must not regress.

Progressive disclosure may reorder or relocate content into folds/one-click reveals but must never delete it — matches R9-NF-1 ('No honesty disclosure deleted') and CLAUDE.md's honesty-as-functional-requirement rule.

Default-open vs. folded state must track importance and length (Few: emphasis by position and weight), not the order features were historically added — this is precisely the failure mode R9 already diagnosed once and must not be allowed to recur on other screens.

Every interactive disclosure (toggle, fold, badge-triggered panel) must carry programmatic state — aria-expanded / aria-controls — not just a visual chevron or label swap, so screen-reader users get the same state signal sighted users get.

The plain-language vocabulary discipline already built in field-copy.ts must cover every rendered enum on every screen — no screen may show a raw internal value (pre_checked, approved as a stage) to a business user.

findings.claim: The register table and its filter chips render raw internal enum values instead of the plain-language labels the rest of the product (field-copy.ts, QuestionnaireStep, GraphView) was specifically rebuilt to provide — directly reproducing the 'too technical' complaint on the screen a 2LoD reviewer scans most.
findings.evidence: "Columns: Use Case Name | Submitter | Tier | Track | Status | Stage | Last Evaluated | Policy Version | Stale | Sampling" ... "Filter chips: High · Medium · Low · Critical · Track II · Track I · pre_checked · approved · Approved with controls · Approved · Rejected" ... "NOTE: raw enum values render in Stage column (\"pre_checked\", \"approved\") and filter chips."
findings.recommendation: Add a STAGE_LABELS map to field-copy.ts (e.g. pre_checked → "Pre-check complete", approved → "Approved") and route the Stage column and its filter chips through the same optionLabel()/*_LABELS pattern already built for QuestionnaireStep and GraphView — this is copy-paste of an existing pattern, not new design work.

findings.claim: Filter chips flatten four unrelated taxonomies — Tier, Track, Stage, Status — into a single undifferentiated row with no grouping, so a user must infer which chip filters what before they can use the filter at all. Few: group related controls; ungrouped controls raise cognitive load before any content is even read.
findings.evidence: "Filter chips: High · Medium · Low · Critical · Track II · Track I · pre_checked · approved · Approved with controls · Approved · Rejected"
findings.recommendation: Break the chip row into labeled clusters — "Tier: Critical / High / Medium / Low", "Track: I / II", "Status: Approved / Approved with controls / Rejected" — each its own <fieldset><legend> group for both visual scanability and screen-reader structure (WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships).

findings.claim: The single longest, most technical block on the page — the full per-rule 'WHY THIS VERDICT' list (12 triggered rules with citations) — renders fully expanded by default, while three shorter, lower-stakes panels immediately below it are folded closed. Disclosure priority is inverted: the biggest cognitive load is unhidden and the small stuff is hidden.
findings.evidence: "WHY THIS VERDICT ... Critical: INV-AUTONOMY-01 ... High: INV-AUTONOMY-02 …[OSFI E-23 §4.3; FCA Consumer Duty PRIN 2A]; INV-CONDUCT-01 …[RAF §4]; INV-DATA-01 …[GDPR Art. 32(1)(a)]; INV-DISCLOSE-01 …; INV-DRIFT-01 …; INV-ESCALATE-01; INV-HALLUC-01 …; INV-TRACK2-01 … Medium: INV-EXPLAIN-01 …; INV-SEC-01 …; INV-SYNTHMARK-01 … Evaluated against 5 hard lines and 18 invariants — 12 triggered." immediately followed by "[fold, closed] ▸ How fragile is this approval? ... [fold, closed] ▸ Platform & vendor inheritance ... [fold, closed] ▸ What would make this verdict expire"
findings.recommendation: Apply the pattern already proven for Similar Cases on GraphView (R9-SC-5: collapse to a count, expand on demand — "2 similar decided cases — show"): keep "Evaluated against 5 hard lines and 18 invariants — 12 triggered" and the single Critical rule (already surfaced separately as the binding constraint) visible by default, fold the full High/Medium rule list behind "show all 12 rules".

findings.claim: The Provisional/review-required status — the one fact a 2LoD reviewer most needs before trusting anything else on the page — is not the first prominent element in reading order; a forward-referencing risk-gap note that points to content far below the fold comes first.
findings.evidence: Reading order per the capture: "[chips] Tier: High · Track: II · Approved with controls · Provisional · pre_checked" then "1 known risk class has no covering rule — see the risk-knowledge panel below." then the tier/track meaning sentences, THEN "[banner] Provisional — review required before this is final / Substantive caveats — real open questions / Cause: no jurisdiction pack applied..."
findings.recommendation: Move the Provisional banner to immediately follow the chip row (Few: position = emphasis for the single most decision-relevant fact). Resolve the 'see risk-knowledge panel below' forward reference by inlining the one-line gap summary at the point of mention — it is already short ("Concentration risk from vendor dependency — Heavy reliance on a single external model vendor concentrates...") — instead of asking the reader to scroll away and back.

findings.claim: The per-card disclosure toggles ('Why these values matter' and 'Edit'/'Done') carry no aria-expanded or aria-controls, so a screen-reader user gets no programmatic signal that the button opens/closes a panel, or which panel it controls — a violation of the toggle-button pattern in Pickering's Inclusive Components and WCAG 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value).
findings.evidence: "<button type=\"button\" className=\"graph-node__why\" onClick={() => setShowWhy((w) => !w)}>{showWhy ? 'Hide why these matter' : 'Why these values matter'}</button>" and "<button type=\"button\" className=\"graph-node__edit\" onClick={onToggleEdit}>{editing ? 'Done' : 'Edit'}</button>" — neither carries aria-expanded (GraphView.tsx)
findings.recommendation: Add aria-expanded={showWhy} plus aria-controls pointing at the consequence <span>'s id to the 'why' button; add the equivalent aria-expanded={editing} and aria-controls to the Edit/Done button pointing at the editor form. Mechanical, no visual change, closes the gap for every field on every card in one pass.

findings.claim: 16 questions (13 required) render as one flat, ungrouped list, even though the underlying data model already has exactly the three-part structure (Input data / Processing / Output) that GraphView renders as three labeled columns two screens later — the submitter is given the mental model once, downstream, instead of twice.
findings.evidence: Flat sequence in the capture — data class, data zone, model type, autonomy, AI run-location, action type, exposure, bindingness, reversibility, platform, vendor, model, decision type, HITL, scale, jurisdictions, with no section headers between them — versus GraphView.tsx's "column('Input data', graph.input_nodes, INPUT_FIELDS) ... column('Processing', graph.processing_nodes, PROCESSING_FIELDS) ... column('Output', graph.output_nodes, OUTPUT_FIELDS)"
findings.recommendation: Group the guided-form fields under the same three headings (plus Jurisdictions) GraphView already uses, each a <fieldset><legend> — reuses an information architecture the product has already committed to, at effectively no design cost.

findings.claim: An unexplained technical status phrase — 'translation fidelity: unattested' — occupies the same persistent, top-of-every-screen position as the product name and the user's own role, for an audience (1LoD) the rest of the product works hard to keep jargon-free. Decoration/noise occupying prime real estate crowds out the information that belongs there (Tufte: everything on the page competes for attention; Few: prominence should track relevance to the current task).
findings.evidence: "Header: AIGate PRE-CHECK ENGINE · policy v1.3 · translation fidelity: unattested · Role [1LoD — James · Dev | 2LoD — Priya · AI Risk]" (captured on the intake screen; capture note states this header is common to all screens)
findings.recommendation: Remove 'translation fidelity: unattested' from the persistent global header. It is only actionable on the Appetite framework screen, which already carries the relevant alert ("ACTION REQUIRED — Starter config in use... translation-fidelity attestation are unfilled") — keep it there, once, where a human can act on it.

findings.claim: All 9 controls render with the full three-line 'What it is / Why this case needs it / What "in place" looks like' shape regardless of status, giving the 8 OUTSTANDING items a submitter must act on the same visual weight as scanning past full detail on every item — there is no summary-first checklist affordance here, even though the identical structural problem was already solved once, on GraphView, by R9-SC-1.
findings.evidence: "What you need to do / Put 9 controls in place... CONTROLS TO PUT IN PLACE / 1. Bounded authority envelope + sampled post-hoc review CTRL-AUTONOMY-BOUND-01 [OUTSTANDING] / What it is: ... Why this case needs it: ... What \"in place\" looks like: ..." repeated for all 9, versus requirements-009.md's R9-SC-1: "A review checklist heads the screen... one line per remaining obligation... each disappearing when done."
findings.recommendation: Port R9-SC-1's pattern (state-derived checklist, one line per OUTSTANDING control, scroll-linked to the full entry, line disappears once IN PLACE) to the top of this screen's control section, exactly as it already works on GraphView — the same requirement, applied to the second screen that has the same problem.

papers.proposed_direction: Apply the R9 pattern — already designed, built, and requirements-tested for GraphView — to the two screens where the identical failure mode is still present unfixed: the verdict/sign-off page and the register list. On the verdict screen, promote the Provisional banner to immediately after the chip row, fold the 12-rule 'why this verdict' detail behind a one-click 'show all rules' the same way Similar Cases was already collapsed to a count, and add a state-derived outstanding-controls checklist at the top the same way GraphView's review checklist works. On the register list, route the Stage column and filter chips through field-copy.ts's existing plain-language pattern, and split the flat chip row into labeled Tier/Track/Status groups. Give the guided intake form the same Input/Processing/Output grouping GraphView already uses downstream, so the mental model is introduced once at intake instead of only appearing later. Close the aria-expanded/aria-controls gap on GraphView's two toggle buttons as a small mechanical accessibility pass, and relocate 'translation fidelity: unattested' out of the persistent global header to the one screen where it's actionable. None of this touches the engine, the policy model, the honesty markers, or removes disclosed content — it is a layout, grouping, and disclosure-ordering pass that finishes applying a pattern the team has already proven works, and it should ship as one coordinated round rather than screen-by-screen, the same way R9 did.

crossExams.panel: Banking practice & the two users (SR 11-7 effective challenge; Emanuel Derman, Models.Behaving.Badly; Cathy O'Neil, Weapons of Math Destruction) — role-played through James (1LoD developer, 10 minutes) and Priya (2LoD AI-risk reviewer, queue of 12)
agreements: Clarity F1 / Information layout F1 / Regulation F4 / AI Governance AIG-5 — all five other panels independently hit the same raw enum leak I flagged as my F2 (pre_checked/approved in the register Stage column and filter chips). Five panels finding the identical defect independently is itself a signal: fix it once, route through field-copy.ts, done.

Interaction Design ID-1 (internal requirement/ADR IDs like LC-2, NF-2, PE-4 rendered inline in end-user prose) — I missed this one in my own round and it's a real James-and-Priya problem: neither user has any use for '(LC-2)' sitting in a sentence, and it's pure engineering exhaust with zero governance value, unlike a rule citation. Agree it should move to a title attribute or footnote, never deleted from the underlying trace.

Regulation F2 and F3 (the self-asserted-identity caveat and the effective-challenge memo's 'restates the record; it does not strengthen it' caption must survive any redesign verbatim, at full visual weight, beside the controls they qualify) — this is exactly the kind of line a friendliness-driven pass would trim first because it 'sounds hedgy,' and it's precisely what Priya needs at the moment she clicks Approve. I'm adopting this as a named exception in my own non-negotiables.

AI Governance AIG-2 (guessed/quoted/no-basis provenance and the no-plain-confirm-on-guessed-cards rule are non-negotiable, not clutter to be simplified away) — matches my own non-negotiable #2 word for word in intent.

Information layout F3/F4 and Regulation F1 (state-derived checklist header at the top of the verdict page; Provisional banner promoted to immediately after the chip row; full 12-rule list folded behind a 'show all rules' with the binding constraint left visible) — this is the R9 pattern applied correctly to the exact screen my own F1 flagged, and I'd rather see one converged design than five near-identical patches landing separately.

Clarity F3 / Interaction Design ID-3 (demote the parenthetical technical code on every guided-form option out of the primary clickable label) — converges with my own F3; James reads roughly 90 parentheticals he doesn't need on his first pass through the form.

AI Governance AIG-7 / Regulation F6 (split the policy screen: plain-English lever cards and jurisdiction status as the default view both roles can read, raw-YAML edit/save gated behind an explicit advanced affordance) — converges with my own F6 almost exactly.

Interaction Design's proposal to make the plain-language/LLM intake path the default entry point rather than something gated behind a Settings visit — this is what James actually wants in his ten minutes, and it raises the stakes on fixing GraphView's badge density (my own F7), since more users will hit that screen as their first real interaction with the graph.

Regulation F5 (flag an unanswered decision-bearing field like decision_type/hitl with the same visual weight as a guessed field, rather than letting it render as indistinguishable 'not stated') — good catch, this is a real SR 11-7 gap: an omission that changes the regulatory analysis currently looks identical to an unremarkable skipped optional field.

objections.about: ID-4: pin the sign-off action bar (name, notes, Approve/Request correction/Challenge) directly under the verdict summary as a sticky element, on the grounds that Fogg's trigger must land while motivation is high
objections.objection: As written, with no role gate, this makes the single worst thing on today's page better for Priya and worse for James at the same time. Today James at least has to scroll past the Approve button to ignore it; under ID-4 he'd land on a page with a big sticky 'Approve' control sitting right under the verdict, on a screen he has no authority to act on. That's not a UX nit — it's the collision my own F1/non-negotiable #4 exists to prevent: sign-off controls becoming reachable, or merely visually prominent, for an unauthorised role.
