Fogg's own model cuts the other way here too: putting the trigger where motivation is high is exactly how you get a reviewer clicking Approve before she's engaged the checklist above it — the 'checking becomes ritual' failure the Regulation panel names in their own F1.
objections.counter_proposal: Merge ID-4 with Regulation F1 and my own F1: render the sticky action bar only when the active role is 2LoD, positioned directly beneath the new state-derived checklist header (not beneath five panels of evidence, and not directly under the bare verdict either). For James, the equivalent fixed position holds his 'what you need to do' summary with no action controls in it at all. One sticky element, two different contents keyed to role — satisfies Fogg's proximity principle for the reviewer who's supposed to act, without ever putting an Approve button in front of someone who can't approve anything.

objections.about: ID-6: fold the 'model confident — no verified basis' badge into the existing 'guessed' visual language, or reword it as task-oriented, because it reads as an alarm with nothing actionable beside it
objections.objection: The reword ('worth a second look — not found in your text') is a clear improvement and I'd take it as-is. But 'fold into guessed' is a different move than a copy change — guessed and no-verified-basis are two structurally distinct provenance states in GraphView.tsx, and only guessed triggers ADR-IF-R6-2 (no plain confirm button, card excluded from the unconfirmed set). If a redesign merges their visual language, the natural next step is merging their gating logic too, and that's exactly the automation-bias regression AI Governance's AIG-2 calls out as the first casualty of a friendliness pass. Derman's whole point — a model is not the truth — is that 'confident but unverified' deserves its own flag precisely because it looks the most trustworthy and is the least checked.
objections.counter_proposal: Take the reword, keep the category structurally separate. Give it its own low-alarm visual treatment (quieter than guessed, since it has no required action, but still a distinct label) rather than either merging it into guessed or leaving it as an unexplained third badge. This is a one-line copy change plus a style tweak, not a logic change, and it keeps AI Governance's non-negotiable intact.

objections.to_panel: Information layout & accessibility (Few, Tufte, WCAG 2.1, Pickering) / Interaction Design
objections.about: F7 / ID-7: remove 'translation fidelity: unattested' from the persistent global header entirely and relocate it solely to the Appetite framework screen, where it's actionable
objections.objection: I agree it's noise for James on his first screen and shouldn't compete with the product name and role switcher. But for Priya, translation fidelity is a live caveat on the confidence of every verdict she's about to sign off on — not just something to fix later on the policy screen. If it disappears from her path entirely until she happens to visit Appetite framework, she can complete a sign-off without ever being told the policy-to-rule translation is unattested, which is precisely the kind of quiet loss of a caveat Michael Power's critique (cited by the Regulation panel) warns is how audit theatre creeps in — individually reasonable trims that add up to a reviewer who signs with less information than she had before.
objections.counter_proposal: Remove the phrase from the persistent masthead (agreed, it's clutter on every screen including intake). But surface it as a small status chip on the verdict/sign-off checklist header specifically — the same header Regulation F1 and I are both proposing — so it travels with the artifact Priya is actually attesting to, not just with the screen where someone could go fix it. One relocation, two destinations: gone from the global header, present at the point of sign-off.

objections.about: F3: drop the parenthetical technical code from the guided form's default rendered option text, reveal it via a 'show technical terms' toggle or hover tooltip
objections.objection: Minor, and I largely agree with the direction (it matches my own F3) — but 'tooltip' as the sole reveal mechanism is thinner than it sounds. A hover-only reveal fails on touch devices James might use, and the Information layout panel's own accessibility standard (WCAG, no info conveyed by hover alone) would flag it if built that way. field-copy.ts's own comment says the term exists specifically so 'a risk or model-validation reader can still map an answer back' — that's Priya's job when she opens the graph-review screen for the same case, not a nice-to-have.
objections.counter_proposal: Render the technical term as an always-visible, low-weight suffix (small muted text, not hidden behind interaction) rather than a hover-only tooltip — reachable on any device, still visually subordinate to the plain-language phrase James actually reads first. This was my own F3 recommendation; flagging it here so it doesn't get built as tooltip-only under Clarity's phrasing.

objections.to_panel: Information layout & accessibility (Few, Tufte, WCAG 2.1, Pickering)
objections.about: F6: group the guided form's 16 fields into fieldset/legend sections mirroring GraphView's Input/Processing/Output columns
objections.objection: Minor process concern, not a content objection — I like the mental-model consistency. But James's whole complaint is a ten-minute budget, and four labeled section headers plus fieldset boundaries can read as four steps rather than one scroll, adding perceived friction even if the field count doesn't change. Worth being deliberate that this stays a single continuous scroll with visual dividers, not a multi-step wizard with per-section navigation, or the 'simplification' will cost James clicks he doesn't have today.
objections.counter_proposal: Implement as in-page section headers/dividers within one continuous scrollable form (no next/back paging), so the Input/Processing/Output grouping aids scanning without adding navigation steps — same fieldset/legend structure Information layout wants for accessibility, just confirmed as non-paginated.

crossExams.revised_position:
Unchanged at the root: targeted redesign, R9 pattern extended to the verdict/sign-off page, register list, and policy screen, nothing in the engine or the honesty apparatus touched. Every other panel converged on the same three screens I flagged, which is the strongest confirmation available that the scope call was right — I'm not revising the verdict, I'm sharpening the plan.

What I'm adding after reading the other five: (1) Interaction Design's ID-1 finding (internal requirement IDs like LC-2/NF-2/PE-4 leaking into user-facing prose) belongs alongside my own F2/F3 as a fourth strip-and-relabel target — it's the same class of bug (system-internal vocabulary rendered as if it were content) and should ship in the same copy-layer pass. (2) I'm formally adopting Regulation's F2 and F3 as named, protected exceptions inside my own non-negotiable #2 — the self-asserted-identity caveat and the effective-challenge memo's self-limiting caption are exactly the two strings most likely to be quietly trimmed by an editor optimizing for 'looks less scary,' and they're load-bearing for the thing Priya's whole job depends on. (3) I'm merging my own F1 with Interaction Design's ID-4 and Regulation's F1 into one concrete design: a state-derived checklist header at the top of the verdict page (binding constraint, jurisdiction status, outstanding-control count, sign-off gate — Regulation's shape), with the sign-off action bar sticky directly beneath it — but role-gated, so James's fixed-position summary never contains an Approve control and Priya's does. That resolves the one real tension in this round: five panels independently reached for 'make the action easier to find' and only my panel was checking whether the audience for that action was authorized to see it at all. Any implementation of ID-4 that ships without that role gate is a regression from today's product, not an improvement, because today's buried-but-present Approve button is at least equally hard for both roles to stumble into.

Two refinements I'm carrying forward as build notes rather than blocking objections: keep the parenthetical technical term on form options always-visible-but-muted, not hover-only (device and accessibility reasons, minor but concrete); and put 'translation fidelity: unattested' on the verdict checklist header where Priya actually needs it, not only on the Appetite framework screen, when it comes out of the global masthead.

Nothing here changes my original findings or non-negotiables — the round confirmed the scope, added one real defect I'd missed (ID-1), and surfaced one design collision (sticky sign-off bar without role gating) that the build must resolve explicitly rather than let five converging 'put it near the top' recommendations quietly ship without the gate my own F1 already specified.

crossExams.panel: Information layout & accessibility (Few, Tufte, WCAG 2.1, Pickering)
agreements: Clarity panel F1 (register Stage column/filter chips render raw enums) — identical to my F1. Same fix: route through a STAGE_LABELS map in field-copy.ts.

Interaction Design panel ID-2 (register enum leakage) and ID-7 (header 'translation fidelity: unattested') — ID-7 is essentially my F7 verbatim; both panels independently landed on removing/relocating that header phrase.

AI Governance panel AIG-5 (register enum leakage) and AIG-1 (hard-line/invariant/jurisdiction-pack trichotomy must stay visually distinct even under a density pass) — AIG-1 is exactly the guardrail my F3 needs: fold the 12-rule list by volume, but the three-category structure inside it must survive the fold, not get flattened into one list to save space.

Regulation & supervisory panel F1 — near-identical diagnosis and near-identical fix to my F3/F8: an R9-SC-1-style checklist header (binding constraint, jurisdiction status, outstanding-control count, sign-off gate) at the top of the verdict page, existing folds left closed. This is convergent, not overlapping — two panels independently re-derived the same pattern from different first principles (mine: position=emphasis; theirs: effective-challenge ritual failure).

Regulation panel F2 (the self-asserted-identity caveat must never be trimmed) and F3 (the effective-challenge memo caption must stay verbatim) — both are direct instances of my non-negotiable #1 (honesty markers stay legible, never softened for a friendlier look). I'm adopting these as explicitly protected strings in any layout pass I do on that screen.

Banker & two-users panel F2 (= my F1) and F4 (Priya's register should default to an 'awaiting my sign-off' view) — F4 doesn't touch my lens directly but it's a good complement to my F2 (grouped filter chips): a smart default view plus well-grouped manual filters solve two different parts of the same scanability problem.

AI Governance panel AIG-7 (move raw YAML editing behind an explicit 'Edit as YAML' affordance, keep lever cards/hard-lines as the default view) — this is the progressive-disclosure principle from my non-negotiables applied correctly: reorder/relocate, nothing deleted, the default view carries the content most users need.

Regulation panel F5 (blank decision-bearing fields should get a quiet badge, same visual family as 'guessed') — good instinct, and I'll hold it to my own non-negotiable #1 (text/icon, never color alone) when it's built.

objections.about: ID-1: 'strip spec-ID citations from rendered strings... carry it as a title attribute, a data attribute, or a footnote reference table'
objections.objection: The 'title attribute' half of this recommendation is not an accessible disclosure mechanism. Native title tooltips are inconsistently exposed to screen readers, never reachable by touch (no hover state on mobile, which the codebase already emulates/tests for), and in most browsers don't appear on keyboard focus at all — so the exact reader who needs to double-check a citation (a 2LoD reviewer tabbing through the page, or anyone on a tablet) loses access to it entirely. This would trade a legibility problem for an access problem, on the same screen the Regulation panel just told us to keep the most defensibility-critical text on.
objections.counter_proposal: Demote spec IDs visually instead of hiding them behind hover: render as a smaller, muted, but still-always-visible inline span (e.g. a footnote-style superscript marker) next to the sentence, or collect them in a single visible 'requirement references' line at the foot of the section. Either satisfies Krug's decluttering goal and stays perceivable without a pointing device — no title attribute, no hover-only content.

objections.about: F6: 'wire the existing TIER_MEANINGS/TRACK_MEANINGS strings as a hover tooltip... directly on the list-view Tier/Track chips'
objections.objection: Same failure mode as above, and it recurs across three papers (Clarity F6, Interaction ID-3's tooltip-for-technical-codes, Banker F3's tooltip framing) — if 'add a hover tooltip' becomes the house fix for every plain-language gap, we ship several new WCAG 1.4.13 (Content on Hover or Focus) failures in the same round meant to fix a complaint about the product being hard to use. A tooltip that isn't dismissible, hoverable, and persistent — which a quick native-title implementation won't be — actively regresses accessibility while looking done in a sighted click-through.
objections.counter_proposal: This is exactly what R9's own pattern already solved once: 'meaning always visible, consequence behind one click.' Don't hide the meaning at all — render the short TIER_MEANINGS/TRACK_MEANINGS phrase as always-visible secondary text directly under or beside the chip (it's one sentence, it fits). Reserve real disclosure widgets — a button with aria-expanded, not a tooltip — for the deeper, multi-sentence consequence text, matching the toggle pattern GraphView already uses for 'Why these values matter.'

objections.about: ID-4: pin/sticky the sign-off action bar directly under the verdict summary
objections.objection: A genuinely fixed/sticky action bar risks permanently occluding page content at high zoom (WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow — 400% zoom on a narrow viewport is exactly when a fixed bar eats the most screen) and can cover whatever element currently has keyboard focus as a user tabs through the page above it (2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured). This is a smaller point than the tooltip issue — easy to get right — but worth naming before anyone builds it as position:fixed without testing zoom and keyboard nav.
objections.counter_proposal: Use a 'jump to sign-off' anchor link near the top instead of (or in addition to) a fixed bar — same Fogg benefit (the trigger for the wanted action is reachable at high motivation) without the occlusion risk. If a sticky bar is still wanted, require it to collapse to a slim tab, or scroll away, above ~200% zoom, and verify no interactive element is ever fully covered by it.

objections.about: ID-6: fold 'model confident — no verified basis' into the existing 'guessed' visual language
objections.objection: This crosses my non-negotiable #1 territory and the AI Governance panel's AIG-2 (the guessed/quoted/no-basis distinction is load-bearing, not decoration). 'Guessed' means the model actively fabricated a value the text doesn't support; 'no verified basis' means the value is plausible but nothing in the source confirms it either way. Those are two different confidence claims a 2LoD reviewer needs to tell apart when deciding what to double-check — merging their labels for tidiness quietly overclaims certainty on one category or underclaims it on the other.
objections.counter_proposal: I.D.'s underlying complaint is fair (it currently reads as an alarm with no button beside it) — fix the actionability, not the taxonomy. Give 'no verified basis' the same badge shape/visual weight as 'guessed' so they read as a visual family, but keep the text label distinct, and reword it toward I.D.'s own suggestion ('worth a second look — not found in your text') while still being a different sentence from the guessed label. Same fix minus the merge.

objections.about: AIG-6: replace the mostly-empty Stale/Sampling columns with an inline badge shown only when the condition is true
objections.objection: Agreed on removing the dead columns, but 'badge only when true, nothing when false' means a screen-reader user gets no signal that the field was even checked and came back clean — a sighted user sees an empty cell and infers 'not stale,' a non-visual user gets nothing to infer from, which is a different (silent) reading of the same row.
objections.counter_proposal: Keep it as a conditional badge visually (agree with AIG-6 on that), but give the badge's container a stable accessible name either way — e.g. an aria-label of 'not flagged as stale' on the empty state, or fold it as a labelled attribute of the row rather than a column that sometimes has content and sometimes doesn't. One line of markup, no visual change.

objections.to_panel: Banking practice & the two users (SR 11-7 / Derman / O'Neil)
objections.about: F1 and F7: role-gated rendering of the sign-off controls, and collapsing confident fields into a one-line per-card summary with only guessed/uncertain fields auto-expanded
objections.objection: Not a real objection, a condition on agreement: both proposals introduce new default-collapsed/default-expanded states, on top of the checklist links Regulation F1 wants and the 'show technical terms' toggle Clarity F3 wants. That's four-plus new disclosure widgets landing in the same round, from four different papers, and not one of them specifies accessible markup for the toggle itself.
objections.counter_proposal: No design change needed — just adopt my non-negotiable #4 as a blanket build requirement for this whole round: every new fold, toggle, badge-triggered panel, or 'show all N' link introduced by any panel's recommendation ships with aria-expanded and aria-controls from day one, the same as I'm requiring for GraphView's two existing toggles (F5). Cheapest possible fix if stated once now, expensive to retrofit six times later.

crossExams.revised_position:
Verdict unchanged: targeted-redesign. Every other panel independently converged on some form of "finish applying the R9 pattern to the verdict page and register list, don't rebuild" — that's five other panels reaching my F3/F8 conclusion from clarity, interaction, governance, regulatory, and two-user angles respectively. I'm treating that convergence as strong confirmation, not just agreement, and folding Regulation F1's framing (checklist header = effective-challenge anchor, not just visual tidiness) into my own rationale for F3/F8 going forward.

What I'm adding to the brief as a result of this meeting: (1) a standing rule that no new disclosure mechanism ships without aria-expanded/aria-controls — this round is about to introduce several (Regulation's checklist links, Clarity's terminology toggle, Banker's per-card collapse, my own F3/F8), and it's cheaper to state once now than fix six times after; (2) an explicit ban on title-attribute and bare-hover tooltips as the delivery mechanism for anything currently proposed that way (Interaction ID-1's spec-ID demotion, Clarity F6's tier/track meanings, the technical-parenthetical toggles in Clarity F3/Interaction ID-3/Banker F3) — the fix in every case is the same: keep short meanings always-visible as secondary text (R9's own "meaning always visible" clause), reserve real focus-reachable disclosure widgets for the longer stuff; (3) a guard on Interaction ID-6's fold-into-guessed proposal — reword for actionability, don't merge the label, because it's the same honesty-marker distinction AIG-2 and my own non-negotiable #1 both call load-bearing.

What I concede: my own paper didn't flag the sticky-action-bar reflow/focus-obscuring risk, the empty-state screen-reader gap in a conditional-badge redesign, or the fact that half the panel proposed tooltip as a delivery mechanism — those are all things I should have caught in Round 1 and only surfaced by reading the other five papers side by side. I also concede that Banker F4's role-aware default register view is a stronger fix for "Priya can't find her queue" than my F2's chip-grouping alone — the two aren't in tension, but F4 should ship alongside F2, not be treated as optional polish on top of it."

agreements: Clarity F1 / Layout F1 / Governance AIG-5 / Regulation F4 / Banking F2 — the register's raw enum leakage ('pre_checked', 'approved' in the Stage column and filter chips) is the clearest, lowest-risk fix on the table. Six of six panels independently flagged it. It's my own ID-2, and I have nothing to add except: ship this first — it's copy-paste of a pattern (field-copy.ts) that already exists, touches no other screen, and every panel agrees it costs nothing.

Clarity F3 / Banking F3 — demoting the inline parenthetical technical term on every guided-form option to a tooltip/toggle, rather than deleting it, is exactly the right shape and resolves a tension I flagged in my own paper (ID-3: 'a control that needs a help paragraph usually needs redesigning'). It also answers Governance's non-negotiable (AIG-3: model/vendor/platform must stay explicit, correctable, first-class) cleanly — the field and its precise value are untouched; only which text is default-visible changes. Presentation-only, Rule 4 compliant, everyone's non-negotiables satisfied at once.

Layout F3 / Regulation F1 / Clarity F4 / Banking F1(partial) — folding the fully-expanded 12-rule 'WHY THIS VERDICT' block behind a 'show all rules' disclosure while keeping the single most-severe rule and the trigger count visible by default is the same move R9 already validated on GraphView, applied one screen over. This directly extends my own ID-4 and I'd merge it into one combined fix rather than build two disclosure mechanisms.

Layout F5 — the missing aria-expanded/aria-controls on GraphView's 'Why these values matter' and Edit/Done toggles is a real gap I didn't catch in Round 1. It's squarely in Krug's territory (a sighted user's chevron state is invisible to a screen-reader user, which is its own 'don't make me think' failure) and it's mechanical to fix. I'm adopting this as an addition to my own findings.

Governance AIG-2's non-negotiable (guessed-card no-confirm gating logic must survive untouched; only chrome/styling may lighten) is fully compatible with my ID-6 — I only asked to reword or fold the 'no verified basis' label into the guessed visual language, never to touch which fields get a confirm affordance. Worth saying explicitly so nobody reads my ID-6 as endorsing a 'confirm all' shortcut, which Governance is right to rule out.

Regulation F2 and Banking's attestation-caveat concerns ('self-asserted, not verified' name field, 'restates the record; does not strengthen it' memo caption) — agreed these must stay full-weight and adjacent to the action, not shrunk. This directly bears on my objection below about role-gating: the same self-asserted-identity fact that Regulation flags as a caveat to protect is also, in my view, a reason not to build UI that pretends role is an access boundary.

objections.about: F1 — 'Render the Approve/Request correction/Challenge block only when the active role is 2LoD -- not merely present-but-ignorable.'
objections.objection: This asks for conditional rendering gated on a role value that the product itself documents as self-asserted and unverified (Regulation panel's own F2/AIG-2 evidence: 'this build has no sign-in, so the name is not verified'). Hard-gating a sign-off control by an unverified role claim doesn't just fail to add security — it actively misrepresents the page as having an access boundary it doesn't have. A submitter who happens to toggle 'role: 2LoD' (however that selector works) would see exactly the same Approve button a real reviewer sees, with nothing distinguishing the two, which is worse than today's honest 'anyone can scroll to it' state because today nothing implies a barrier exists. It also creates a real usability risk for Priya: if role detection is stale, wrong, or resets on reload, her sign-off controls vanish entirely with no fallback — Fogg's trigger has to be reliably present when her motivation is high, and a role-state bug is exactly the kind of thing that silently removes it. This is the same problem NF-2/NF-7 already name for other parts of the product: don't let the UI claim more certainty (here, about identity/authorization) than the system can prove.
objections.counter_proposal: Get the same outcome — Priya doesn't wade through five panels to sign off, James never sees a control he shouldn't click — without conditional-rendering-by-claimed-identity. Default-collapse everything from 'WHY THIS VERDICT' onward behind one 'Show full reasoning & evidence' disclosure (this is Layout F3 / Regulation F1's fix, which I already agree with), and pin a compact sign-off action bar directly under the verdict summary, visible to everyone, exactly as today. Nothing is hidden by role; it's hidden by default-collapsed state, which any viewer can expand — a disclosure choice, not an access-control claim. If the team later adds real authentication, THEN role-gating becomes honest and this objection dissolves on its own.

objections.about: F6 — 'gate the raw-YAML edit/save control behind 2LoD the same way rule challenges already are.'
objections.objection: Same root problem as above, one level lower stakes since YAML editing isn't the defensibility-critical action Approve is. Gating a Save button by a self-asserted role field is theater, not protection — a 1LoD developer curious enough to open Settings and flip the role selector could edit the firm's risk appetite YAML with a UI that visually implies they can't.
objections.counter_proposal: Separate the read-only lever-card / hard-line / jurisdiction-status view (default landing, all roles, matches Governance AIG-7) from the raw-YAML 'Edit as YAML' affordance via information architecture, not access control — don't put an 'Edit as YAML' link in the 1LoD-facing nav at all, the same way the product already keeps the pack-authoring workflow out of the main flow per CLAUDE.md. If the team wants real enforcement later, that's an auth-layer project, not a redesign-brief item.

objections.about: F6 — reusing GraphView's exact 'Input data / Processing / Output' column headers as the guided intake form's section groupings.
objections.objection: I like the underlying move (grouping 16 flat fields into 3-4 sections is my own ID-3), but Input/Processing/Output is itself systems/data-flow vocabulary — it's the engine's mental model of a graph, not a submitter's mental model of the thing they built. Reusing it verbatim risks reintroducing exactly the 'engine's canonical vocabulary wearing a costume' problem my Round-1 paper flagged for the flat form, just one level up at the section-header instead of the field-label.
objections.counter_proposal: Keep the three/four-way split (it's a good, cheap reuse of a structure the product already committed to) but write the headers in the submitter's language — 'What it uses' / 'What it does' / 'Who sees the result' — with 'Input data / Processing / Output' as a small secondary label only if the team wants visual continuity with GraphView for the 2LoD reader who sees both screens.

crossExams.revised_position:
I'm not moving off targeted-redesign, and reading the other five papers mostly hardened rather than changed my Round-1 findings — five other panels landing independently on the register-enum leak, the verdict page's buried sign-off, and the parenthetical-jargon problem is about as strong a signal as this format produces that those three are real and worth fixing first. Concretely, I'm merging my ID-4 (pin the sign-off action bar) with Layout F3 / Regulation F1's fold-the-rule-list proposal into a single change rather than two: default-collapsed 'full reasoning' disclosure plus a pinned compact action bar, available to every viewer regardless of role. I'm adding Layout F5 (aria-expanded/aria-controls on GraphView's toggles) to my findings outright — I missed it, it's cheap, and it's squarely Krug's territory for assistive-tech users.

Two things I'm conceding on reflection, not from another panel's objection but from Regulation's own evidence: my ID-3 lumped decision_type into the same 'progressive disclosure / advanced toggle' bucket as platform and vendor. Regulation's F5 is right that decision_type (and hitl) are materially decision-bearing — hiding them behind an advanced fold makes it easier to skip them unnoticed, which is the opposite of what a submitter needs. I'm narrowing ID-3: only platform and vendor (genuinely peripheral metadata) go behind progressive disclosure; decision_type and hitl stay in the primary flow with their existing 'leave blank only if...' guidance intact and, ideally, get the same quiet not-guessed-but-not-answered visual flag Regulation F5 proposes on the graph-review card.

My one live disagreement is with Banking's F1 and F6: role-gating the sign-off controls (and the YAML editor) by a self-asserted, unverified role value trades a real usability win for a fake security claim, which is exactly the kind of overclaiming CLAUDE.md's honesty rule and the Regulation panel's own attestation-caveat findings warn against elsewhere on the same page. My counter-proposal gets Banking's actual goal — Priya isn't buried, James doesn't see controls that aren't his to use — through default-collapsed disclosure state instead of conditional rendering keyed to an identity claim nothing verifies. Everything else — the register fix, the parenthetical-to-tooltip move, the masthead relocation, the rule-list folding, the graph-review label reuse — I'd ship as originally proposed, now with five more sets of eyes confirming none of it touches the engine, the audit trail, or a single honesty disclosure.

agreements: Interaction Design ID-2, Information layout & accessibility F1, AI Governance AIG-5, Regulation F4, and Banking F2 all independently landed on the same defect as my own F1: raw enum values ('pre_checked', 'approved') rendering verbatim in the register's Stage column and filter chips. Six-panel unanimity on one finding is rare — this should be the first chunk built, no debate needed.

Interaction Design ID-1 and my F5 both call for stripping internal spec/requirement-tracking IDs (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4) out of rendered prose. I want to sharpen the shared recommendation, not just agree with it: this must stay categorically separate from the Regulation panel's non-negotiable that regulatory citations (OSFI E-23 §4.3, GDPR Art 32(1)(a)) stay attached and visible. Same instinct ('there's a bracketed code in this sentence, cut it'), opposite target — an implementer moving fast could conflate the two and strip citations along with spec IDs. Worth saying explicitly in the combined brief.

Information layout & accessibility F3 and Regulation F1 both propose an R9-SC-1-style checklist header for the verdict page with the full rule list folded behind a 'show all rules' reveal. This is a better-scoped version of my own F4 (which only restructured the WHY block's internal shape) — I'm adopting their framing over mine.

Interaction Design ID-6 (the unglossed third confidence category 'model confident — no verified basis' sitting beside 'guessed' with no action attached) is a clean catch I didn't make myself but is squarely in my lane — Podmajersky's rule that a label implies an action, and this one implies none.

Regulation F2 and F3 (protect the self-asserted-identity caveat and the effective-challenge memo's 'restates the record; does not strengthen it' caption at full weight, exempt from any copy-shortening pass) reinforce my own non-negotiable about never softening honesty disclosures for friendliness. I'll fold their two specific protected strings into our shared brief as named exceptions.

Information layout & accessibility F6 and Banking F5's field-grouping proposals (Input/Processing/Output sections on the guided form, mirroring GraphView's existing column structure) strengthen my own F3 — grouping plus my toggle-based fix for the parenthetical codes are complementary, not competing, fixes for the same screen.

objections.about: ID-4 (pin sign-off action bar near top for 2LoD, distinct from 1LoD's 'what you need to do')
objections.objection: Fine as a default-state change, but Banking's F1 takes the same idea further and renders the Approve/Request-correction/Challenge block conditionally on 'the active role' — and the register's own header shows role is a self-selected dropdown next to a name field the app itself labels 'not verified, this build has no sign-in.' Gating a visible control on that toggle doesn't make sign-off safer, it just teaches the reader that switching a dropdown changes what actions are available to them — which reads as real access control where none exists. That's a message the UI would be making that isn't true, and an honesty problem is worse than a density problem.
objections.counter_proposal: Keep the full page reachable in both role views — no control is ever removed from the DOM based on role. Change only the DEFAULT open/closed state: in '1LoD view' the reasoning/sign-off section renders collapsed behind a labeled expander ('For your 2LoD reviewer — full reasoning & sign-off'); in '2LoD view' it's expanded by default. Same scan-time win Interaction Design and Banking are both after, without implying an enforcement boundary the product doesn't have. Label the toggle itself as a view preference, not a permission.

objections.about: F1 (render Approve/Request correction/Challenge block only when active role is 2LoD) and F6 (gate raw-YAML policy editor behind 2LoD the same way rule challenges already are)
objections.objection: Same root problem as above, doubled for F6: hiding the Save control from '1LoD view' on the policy screen could be read by a first-time user as 'the system enforces this,' when a name field with an explicit 'not verified' disclosure two screens over says the opposite. If this ships as visual-only gating, it needs to say so at the point of the gate, or it quietly overclaims the product's access-control maturity — the exact kind of overclaim CLAUDE.md's honesty rule forbids for engine output and that I'd hold rendered UI to as well.
objections.counter_proposal: Same fix as above: default-collapse rather than hard-hide, with a one-line note near the collapsed section ('shown to 2LoD reviewers by default — anyone can expand this') that is honest about what the toggle actually does. If real role enforcement is wanted later, that's a separate, larger piece of work than this redesign round and shouldn't be implied by copy/layout alone.

objections.about: F1's worked example for the new STAGE_LABELS map — explicitly proposes approved → 'Approved'
objections.objection: This recreates, in the very fix meant to clean up the register, the exact regression CLAUDE.md's gotcha section warns about: 'the verdict screen is asserted with a single-match /approved|rejected/i query... avoid those two words in any new rendered string.' Once Stage is glossed and rendered as its own visible label next to Status (which may already read 'Approved' or 'Approved with controls' on the same row), the page now has two independent elements matching that regex where before it may have had one relying on a specific selector. This is exactly the class of bug the note says 'has misled subagent reviews more than once' — a redesign fixing jargon shouldn't reintroduce a known test-fragility trap in the same commit.
objections.counter_proposal: Map Stage's 'approved' value to a word that doesn't reuse Status's vocabulary at all — my own F1 proposed 'Signed off'; 'Finalised' or 'Complete' would work equally well. More generally: every STAGE_LABELS / label-map value proposed across all six panels' findings needs an /approved|rejected/i check before it lands, not just this one entry — worth calling out as a single shared gate on the combined implementation chunk rather than trusting each screen's fix to remember it independently.

objections.about: ID-7 (remove 'translation fidelity: unattested' from the persistent header entirely, move it solely to About/Settings or a small tooltip chip) — Information layout & accessibility F7 makes the same move, relocating it solely to the Appetite framework screen
objections.objection: This phrase isn't a per-case caveat, it's a pack-level honesty disclosure that currently reaches a 2LoD reviewer on every screen, including the verdict page where they're about to sign off on a case governed by that same pack. If it lives only on the Policy/Appetite screen, a reviewer who works entirely from the register and never opens that screen loses the signal at exactly the moment it's most load-bearing for defensibility — this is the Regulation panel's own non-negotiable ('provisional/unverified must stay visually inseparable from the verdict or control it qualifies') applied one level up, at the pack rather than the case. Deleting it from the reading path a reviewer actually takes is a real loss dressed up as a trunk-test win.
objections.counter_proposal: Compress, don't relocate-and-forget: shrink the header phrase to a small chip with a tooltip carrying the full sentence — both panels already point at the right precedent themselves (the existing 'pending adoption' pack chips). Additionally surface a one-line version on the verdict page itself, next to the jurisdiction-pack status note that's already there, so the disclosure survives at the point of decision even for a reviewer who never visits the Policy screen. This keeps Krug's trunk test win at the top of every page without breaking the disclosure-stays-with-the-decision rule.

objections.about: ID-2's aside questioning 'whether Stage needs to exist as a distinct column from Status at all'
objections.objection: Minor, but worth flagging before an implementer reads this as license to drop a column: Stage and Status may be genuinely different taxonomies (workflow position vs. decision content) rather than redundant labels for the same fact — collapsing them without checking could silently delete information a reviewer needs (e.g. 'what happens next' vs 'what was decided'), which would violate R9's own aggregate-or-one-click-away-never-delete precedent that every panel including Interaction Design's own paper cites as the binding pattern.
objections.counter_proposal: Before merging, confirm with the product owner whether Stage conveys anything Status doesn't. If it's genuinely redundant, fold it into a secondary line under Status rather than deleting the column outright — same R9 move, applied here instead of assumed away.

crossExams.revised_position:
Unchanged at the root: targeted-redesign, same three screens (register list, verdict/sign-off WHY section, guided intake form), same non-negotiables. Nothing in the other five papers gave me a reason to widen scope to a full redesign — if anything, the near-unanimous convergence on the register-enum bug and the verdict-page density problem confirms the R9 pattern is the right lever and just needs to be finished, not replaced.

What I'm adopting from the room: broaden my F4 from 'restructure the WHY block's internal shape' to the fuller R9-SC-1 checklist header that Information layout & accessibility (F3) and Regulation (F1) both specified — binding constraint, jurisdiction status, outstanding-control count, sign-off gate, each scrolling to its section, full rule list folded behind one click. That's a strictly better version of what I proposed alone. I'm also adopting Information layout & accessibility's F6 grouping of the guided form into Input/Processing/Output sections as the right container for my own toggle-based fix to the parenthetical codes (F3) — group first, then demote the technical term inside each group, rather than treating grouping and de-jargoning as competing proposals. And I'm folding Regulation's F2/F3 protected strings (self-asserted-identity caveat, effective-challenge memo caption) into our shared brief as explicit, named exceptions to any copy-shortening pass, since they're exactly the kind of thing a well-meaning editor cuts first.

What I'm holding the line on: role-based hiding of the sign-off controls or the policy-edit controls (Interaction Design ID-4, Banking F1/F6) has to become role-based *default disclosure state*, not conditional rendering — the product has no real authentication, and a control that visually disappears based on a self-selected dropdown teaches the reader a false thing about the system's access control, which is a bigger honesty problem than the one this whole redesign is trying to fix. Same principle, opposite direction, for the translation-fidelity marker (Interaction Design ID-7, Information layout & accessibility F7): compress it, don't strip it from the decision-time reading path, because it's a pack-level provisional marker and the Regulation panel's own non-negotiable says exactly that kind of marker has to stay attached to the decision it qualifies. And I'm flagging, as a blocking issue for whoever writes the actual implementation chunk: Information layout & accessibility's own worked example (approved → 'Approved') would recreate the CLAUDE.md /approved|rejected/i test-fragility gotcha in the very fix meant to clean up the register — every label-map value proposed across all six papers needs that regex check before it ships, as one shared gate on the combined chunk rather than six independent screens each trusting themselves to remember it.

Net effect on scope: no new screens added, no screens dropped, same handful of focused chunks I proposed in round 1 — the meeting sharpened the verdict-page fix (adopt the fuller checklist pattern), added one reusable gate (reserved-word check on every new label), and drew one bright line (default state, never conditional rendering, for anything framed as 'role-gating' on a product with no real auth).

crossExams.panel: AI Governance (NIST AI RMF · Stuart Russell · Mitchell et al. Model Cards · OWASP LLM Top-10 · Christoph Molnar)
agreements: Clarity F1/F5 and Interaction Design ID-1/ID-2 and Information layout F1: strip internal requirement-tracking IDs (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4, R-numbers) from rendered prose and map the register's Stage enum to plain labels. This is pure engineering exhaust, matches our own AIG-5/AIG-6, and costs nothing governance-wise since none of these tokens carry regulatory or provenance weight.

Regulation panel's non-negotiables are effectively our own, restated from the supervisory side: citations inseparable from the rule line, Provisional/UNVERIFIED inseparable from the verdict/control it qualifies, append-only audit trail never filtered from default view, named sign-off kept distinct with its self-asserted caveat attached, three-lever separation preserved. We treat these as jointly owned between our two panels and will defend them together.

Regulation F2 and F3 (protect the self-asserted-identity caveat and the effective-challenge memo's 'restates the record; does not strengthen it' caption verbatim, exempt from any copy-shortening pass) — this is exactly the audit-theatre failure mode Power and our own overclaiming non-negotiable both warn about. Full agreement, no changes.

Regulation F5 (flag a blank decision-bearing field like decision_type/hitl with the same visual weight as a guessed field, rather than letting it render as an unremarkable 'not stated') — this closes a real gap in our own AIG-3 finding and gives us a better answer than hiding these fields entirely.

Information layout F5/F6 and AI Governance AIG-7 converge independently on the same fix: separate the raw-YAML editor from the human-readable lever cards/citation view on the policy screen, and give the guided form the Input/Processing/Output grouping GraphView already uses downstream. Agreed — reuses an IA the product already committed to.

Interaction Design ID-8 and Clarity F7 (reuse the existing plain-English gloss for 'invariants' in the compact stat line instead of the bare term two lines above its own translation) — a clean drift-fix, no content lost.

Banking practice F2/F4 (route Priya to a default 'awaiting my sign-off' view built from a number the register already computes) — this is a workflow-queue improvement that strengthens effective challenge (a reviewer who has to hand-assemble filter chips every session is more likely to miss a case) rather than weakening it.

objections.about: Finding ID-6 — 'fold [model confident — no verified basis] into the existing guessed visual language'
objections.objection: These are not the same epistemic state and collapsing them is a governance regression dressed as a UI simplification. 'Guessed' means the model told the reader it doesn't know. 'Confident — no verified basis' means the model asserted something with conviction and nothing in the source text backs it — this is precisely the OWASP LLM Top-10 case (output is untrusted input) and the Molnar case (an explanation that reads as certain but isn't is worse than one that visibly hedges) where under-scrutiny is most dangerous. A guessed badge already carries a 'fix it' affordance; folding the confident-no-basis case into that visual language either gives it an affordance it doesn't need (it isn't a blank to fill in) or, worse, makes it look like ordinary guessed-and-handled content and gets less attention than it currently gets as its own alarm.
objections.counter_proposal: Keep it a visually distinct third category, but make it actionable rather than merely present: give it a short one-click 'double-check this against the source' affordance (parallel to, not merged with, the guessed badge's 'correct it' affordance). That satisfies Interaction Design's complaint that it's currently an alarm with nothing to do, without erasing the distinction that matters most for hallucination risk.

objections.about: Finding ID-4 — pin the sign-off action bar directly under the verdict summary with the full rules audit reachable only via a jump link
objections.objection: Literally relocating Approve/Request correction/Challenge to sit right after the headline verdict, with the citation-backed reasoning demoted to an optional jump-away, invites exactly the SR 11-7 rubber-stamp failure our panel exists to prevent: a reviewer can motivationally click Approve at the moment Fogg says intent is highest, precisely because the friction of reading the reasoning has been removed. A sign-off control that's easier to reach than the evidence it certifies is a worse design than one that's harder to reach, for this specific product.
objections.counter_proposal: Adopt the Regulation panel's and Information-layout panel's version instead: an R9-style checklist at the top of the page (binding constraint, jurisdiction status, outstanding-control count, sign-off gate) that IS the compressed reasoning, not a bypass of it — each line still names the rule and citation, just at summary weight. Keep the name/notes/Approve controls reachable without a long scroll (sticky footer is fine), but do not let them sit above a page that has stripped the reasoning down to a jump link.

objections.about: Finding F1 — 'render the Approve/Request correction/Challenge block only when the active role is 2LoD'
objections.objection: This build has no authentication — role is self-asserted (the same fact Regulation F2 and our own attestation non-negotiable are built around). A UI that hard-renders sign-off controls based on 'active role' implies an access-control boundary that does not exist: anyone can flip a role selector and get the Approve button. Presenting this as gating rather than as a view preference overclaims what the system can actually enforce, which is the exact overclaiming our non-negotiables forbid.
objections.counter_proposal: Keep it a soft default (collapse the full dossier under 'what you need to do' for a 1LoD-style view, expand it under a 2LoD-style view) rather than hard-rendering or hiding the sign-off controls themselves. Label the role toggle explicitly as a display preference, and keep 'self-asserted — this build has no sign-in' visible next to it, not just next to the name field on the Approve form.

objections.about: Finding ID-3 — put the three 'optional' fields (platform, vendor, decision type) behind an advanced toggle
objections.objection: Vendor and platform are not cosmetic optional fields from a governance standpoint — they're the data our own invariant text cites verbatim ('AI model versions must be pinned and outputs monitored for silent substitution', INV-TRACK2-01) and are exactly what Mitchell et al.'s model-card principle says must travel with the model. Decision type is flagged separately by the Regulation panel (F5) as materially changing the regulatory analysis when left blank. Hiding all three behind 'advanced' next to genuinely cosmetic settings risks submitters skipping fields that change the verdict, not just the form's length.
objections.counter_proposal: Keep these three at primary visual weight but give them the plain-language treatment field-copy.ts already does well elsewhere. Where a field is genuinely left blank, use Regulation F5's badge (equal weight to the guessed badge) rather than a folder toggle — that surfaces omission as a fact to notice, instead of letting 'advanced' collapse make omission look like nothing was hidden at all.

objections.about: Finding F8 — outstanding-control checklist line 'disappearing when done'
objections.objection: This is very likely just phrasing, but as written it's ambiguous between 'moves out of the still-to-do list' and 'is removed from the page,' and the second reading directly conflicts with our UNVERIFIED-controls non-negotiable: a control a submitter has clicked 'in place' on is self-reported, not evidenced, and must not visually vanish as if resolved.
objections.counter_proposal: Item moves from the 'still outstanding' checklist into a 'addressed' sub-section (or gets struck through, not deleted), and wherever it renders — checklist or full control list below — its evidence status (UNVERIFIED unless someone attaches evidence) stays attached to it. Same visual pattern, one word of clarification in the spec.

objections.about: Finding ID-2 — 'question whether Stage needs to exist as a distinct column from Status at all'
objections.objection: Stage (workflow position: pre_checked vs. signed off) and Status (verdict outcome: approved with controls, provisional) answer different questions, and the workflow-position one is exactly what Banking practice's own F4 proposal (default Priya's register to 'awaiting my sign-off') depends on existing as queryable data. Merging them to reduce column count would remove the dimension that fix needs.
objections.counter_proposal: Relabel, don't merge: Stage becomes a plain-language phrase ('Awaiting 2LoD sign-off' / 'Signed off') alongside Status, both routed through the same label map. Keeps two real facts legible instead of collapsing them into one that can't answer 'what's still mine to do.'

crossExams.revised_position:
I'm not moving off any of our six non-negotiables, and having read all five other papers I'm more confident they don't need to move either — Regulation's paper in particular is close enough to ours that I'd merge our two non-negotiable lists into one shared appendix for whoever builds this, rather than let two overlapping-but-differently-worded versions drift apart across chunks.

What I concede: four independent panels (Interaction Design, Information layout, Regulation, Banking practice) converged on the same diagnosis for the verdict page — a fully-expanded wall of reasoning above a buried sign-off action is bad for both personas, not just the 1LoD one I was originally focused on defending against dilution. I was too quick in round 1 to treat 'more visible reasoning' as strictly safer; Power's audit-theatre point cuts the other way too — a reviewer who has stopped reading a wall of text because it's always the same wall of text is not more defensible than one reading a well-structured summary. I now recommend the R9-checklist-at-top approach (Regulation F1, Information-layout F3/F8) over the status quo, with the specific correction that the checklist itself carries the rule names and citations at summary weight — it's a compression of the reasoning, not a bypass link around it, which is the distinction that matters to me.

I also concede the raw-YAML-as-default-view problem (my own AIG-7, echoed by Information layout F6 and Banking practice F6) should be fixed in the same round as the other screens rather than treated as separate — all three of us independently flagged it, which tells me it's a real, not a manufactured, priority.

What I'm holding firm on, unchanged by anything I read: the three per-field epistemic states (quoted / guessed / confident-no-basis) stay three states, not two; vendor/platform/decision_type stay primary-weight fields, not advanced-toggle fields; any role-based UI behavior is described and built as a view preference, never as access control, until this product has real authentication; and 'outstanding control' checklist items move, they never vanish. These four points go into the shared implementation brief as explicit call-outs, because they're exactly the kind of thing a well-intentioned copy-and-layout pass could quietly erode without anyone deciding to erode them.

crossExams.panel: Regulation & supervisory defensibility (PRA SS1/23, SR 26-2, EU AI Act, OSFI E-23, MAS FEAT, Michael Power)
agreements: Every panel independently converged on 'extend R9, don't rebuild' as the verdict — that convergence itself is useful evidence for the owner: five different lenses looked at the same screens and none found a reason to touch the engine, the audit model, or the disclosure content. Worth saying plainly in the readout.

Clarity F1 / Interaction Design ID-2 / Information Layout F1 / AI Governance AIG-5 / Banking F2 — all independently found the register's raw enum leakage ('pre_checked', 'approved' as Stage) and want it routed through field-copy.ts's label-map pattern. Agree without reservation; the raw enum should stay retrievable (tooltip/data-attribute) for anyone reconciling against the audit trail, but it has no business being the primary label a reviewer reads.

AI Governance AIG-4 — attach the 'advisory — not required for sign-off' qualifier to the risk-knowledge gap line at its FIRST mention (top of verdict page), not only in the panel below. This directly reinforces my own non-negotiable #5 (three-lever separation must be visible everywhere it appears, not just in the panel that happens to have room for the caveat). Strong agree.

AI Governance AIG-7 / Banking F6 — split the raw-YAML policy editor from the human-readable lever-cards/hard-lines/jurisdiction-status view, and gate the editor separately. This is the same finding as my own F6, argued independently from a governance and a banking-practice angle. Agree, with one refinement in my objections below.

AI Governance AIG-2 (critical) — keep the guessed/quoted/no-basis gating exactly as-is, and explicitly reject any 'confirm all' shortcut that could clear a guessed field. This is the same mechanism my F5 is protecting from the opposite direction (blank decision-bearing fields need the same visual seriousness as guessed fields, not less). Strong agree — these are two faces of one principle: silence and guessing are both states that must stay visible, never smoothed into 'looks answered.'

Interaction Design ID-1 / Clarity F5 — strip internal requirement/ADR tracking codes (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4, R-numbers) out of rendered prose. Agree these are pure engineering exhaust, not regulatory content — worth being explicit that this is a different category from the citations in my non-negotiable #1 (SS1/23 §3.4, GDPR Art 32(1)(a), etc.), which must stay. See objection below on the risk of an implementer conflating the two.
Information Layout F5 (aria-expanded/aria-controls on GraphView's two toggle buttons) — purely additive, mechanical, no content or disclosure implication. Agree, no notes.

Information Layout F6 / Banking F7-adjacent — group the guided form into Input/Processing/Output sections matching GraphView's existing structure. No defensibility concern; agree this is a free win that also makes the graph-review screen (where the actual confirmation happens) feel continuous with the form the submitter just filled out.

objections.about: ID-4: pin the sign-off action bar (name, notes, Approve/Request correction/Challenge) directly under the verdict summary as a sticky element, with the full reasoning reachable only via a jump link, justified by 'the trigger for the wanted action must land while motivation is high, not after a long scroll of caveats that can talk a reviewer out of finishing.'
objections.objection: This is precisely the mechanism Michael Power's audit-society critique warns about: an attestation control positioned to be clicked before the thing it attests to has been read. SS1/23 effective challenge exists to make sure a 2LoD reviewer's sign-off reflects actual engagement with the reasoning, not proximity to a button. Framing the caveats and citation chain as friction 'that can talk a reviewer out of finishing' inverts what that content is for — if reading the reasoning changes a reviewer's mind about approving, that is the system working, not a UX defect to route around. A sticky Approve button one scroll below the summary, on a page whose own content includes 12 triggered rules and 9 outstanding controls, invites exactly the ritual-checking failure mode this panel is watching for.
objections.counter_proposal: Keep IxD's underlying instinct (don't make the reviewer hunt for the sign-off fields) but change the mechanism: put a sticky mini-nav (not the Approve button itself) that jumps between sections — Verdict / Why / Controls / Sign-off — mirroring the checklist header my own F1 proposes. The name/notes fields can stay visually anchored near the top as a 'you'll sign off at the bottom' preview, but the actual Approve control stays positioned after the reasoning content, or is gated behind having opened the checklist items (same one-click-away pattern R9 already uses elsewhere, just applied as a soft gate rather than a hard block). This gets Fogg's 'don't lose the motivated moment' benefit without letting the trigger outrun the review.

objections.to_panel: Information layout & accessibility (Few, Tufte, WCAG 2.1, Pickering)
objections.about: F3: fold the full 'WHY THIS VERDICT' list (12 triggered rules with citations) behind a 'show all 12 rules' click, leaving only the single Critical rule and a count visible by default — modeled on the Similar Cases collapse-to-count pattern.
objections.objection: Similar Cases is reference material; the 12-rule list is the evidentiary chain the verdict is actually reasoning from — it is the one thing on this page a supervisor doing SS1/23-style effective-challenge review would ask to see in full without an extra click, and my non-negotiable #6 says this chain must 'stay traceable end to end.' Defaulting to showing only 1 of 12 triggered rules risks a reviewer signing off having seen a Critical item but not knowing 8 High/Medium items with independent citations (OSFI E-23 §4.3, GDPR Art. 32(1)(a), EU AI Act Art. 50(1)) exist at all unless they think to click through.
objections.counter_proposal: Apply Clarity's own F4 fix here instead of Information Layout's fold: give each of the 12 rules a compact one-line default rendering — plain rule name + citation marker, e.g. 'Autonomy escalation missing [OSFI E-23 §4.3]' — all 12 lines visible by default (this is what the controls list already does at 9 items with three-line detail; a one-line list of 12 is not longer than that). Fold only the extended prose explanation per rule behind a click, not the existence and citation of the rule itself. This gets Information Layout's density win — the page stops being one dense unstructured paragraph — without dropping 11 citations below the fold.

objections.to_panel: Information layout & accessibility (Few, Tufte, WCAG 2.1, Pickering)
objections.about: F7, echoed by Interaction Design ID-7: remove 'translation fidelity: unattested' from the persistent global header entirely, keeping it only on the Appetite framework screen where it is 'actionable.'
objections.objection: This status is not decorative — it tells the reader whether the rulebook's translation from policy text into machine-checkable invariants has been verified, which bears directly on how much weight to put on any citation shown on the verdict page in front of them right now. Removing it from every screen except the one where a pack author would fix it means the 2LoD reviewer signing off on a specific case, on the specific screen where they're weighing citations, loses the one signal that says 'those citations rest on an unattested translation.' That is an NF-7-class honesty disclosure being pulled from the screen where it matters most to the reader who needs it, not just decluttered.
objections.counter_proposal: Compress, don't remove: replace the spelled-out header phrase with a small persistent chip (e.g. a single warning glyph + 'v1.3 unattested', expandable on click/hover for the full sentence) on every screen that shows a verdict or citation. Drop the full sentence only from screens with no verdict content (About, pure navigation) — which is most of what Information Layout's own complaint is really about.

objections.about: ID-3: progressively disclose platform, vendor, AND decision type behind an 'advanced' toggle, treating all three as equally low-priority optional fields.
objections.objection: This groups a field with real regulatory weight in with two that don't. field-copy.ts's own consequence text for decision_type says 'Names the decision the rulebook must cover. Credit and lending decisions carry the highest floors' — and my own F5 already flags that decision_type and hitl are decision-bearing fields whose silent omission changes the regulatory analysis with no comparable visual flag to a guessed field. Hiding them behind an 'advanced' toggle by default makes the omission easier to happen unnoticed, not harder — the opposite of what F5 is asking for.
objections.counter_proposal: Split the three: platform and vendor (genuinely low-stakes optional context) go behind progressive disclosure as IxD proposes. decision_type and hitl stay default-visible with their existing guidance ('leave blank only if it feeds no decision at all') attached, and — per my own F5 — an unanswered render of either gets the same quiet flag a guessed field gets on the graph-review screen, so a reviewer downstream can see the omission was rendered, not silently defaulted-away.

objections.about: F2: collapse the 'Approved with controls · Provisional · pre_checked' chip stack into a single paraphrased lead sentence ('Not final — 2 second-line reviews and 2LoD sign-off still needed'), demoting the literal chips to a secondary line.
objections.objection: The literal verdict value ('Approved with controls') paired with its qualifier ('Provisional') is the actual data-model status string that also appears in the register and, eventually, the audit trail — my non-negotiable #2 requires that pairing stay visually inseparable wherever the verdict renders, not merely implied by a paraphrase. A friendlier lead sentence is a good addition, but if it fully replaces the literal chip pair rather than sitting beside it, a reader comparing this screen against the register row or an export loses the direct textual match between what they're looking at and what's recorded.
objections.counter_proposal: Additive, not substitutive: keep Clarity's plain-English lead sentence as the new first line, but keep the literal 'Approved with controls · Provisional' pair directly beside or below it in the same visual unit — drop only 'pre_checked' (the internal stage token, which nobody outside engineering needs) from this particular chip row, consistent with the register-list fix everyone already agrees on.

objections.about: ID-1's non-negotiable groups internal spec IDs (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4) and regulatory citations under one instinct ('strip parenthetical IDs from prose'), with the same bracket/paren convention used for both in the evidence quotes.
objections.objection: I agree the internal IDs should go (see Agreements) — but the evidence for ID-1 quotes '(PE-4)' and '(NF-2)' in the same breath as bracketed regulatory citations like '[OSFI E-23 §4.3]' elsewhere on the same page. If an implementer builds one 'strip parenthetical technical-looking codes' pass rather than two deliberately distinct ones, a regulatory citation is one regex tweak away from being caught in the same net as an internal req ID — which would violate my non-negotiable #1.
objections.counter_proposal: Make the two conventions visually and structurally distinct before anyone touches the code: regulatory citations render as their own tagged element (a citation chip/pill, already partially true with the bracket style) that a 'remove internal IDs' pass is explicitly scoped to exclude; internal req/ADR IDs (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4, HL-*, VD-4) get deleted outright, not just visually restyled. Naming this distinction in the implementation ticket avoids the ambiguity.

objections.to_panel: AI Governance (NIST AI RMF · Stuart Russell · Mitchell et al. Model Cards · OWASP LLM Top-10 · Christoph Molnar)
objections.about: AIG-7 (and Banking F6, which makes it explicit): gate the raw-YAML policy editor behind a '2LoD' role check, mirroring the existing 'Rule challenges (2LoD only)' sidebar gating.
objections.objection: CLAUDE.md's own rule is that pack/rule authoring is 'human-led, never generated' — it doesn't say '2LoD-led.' A 2LoD case reviewer signing off on individual use cases is not automatically the same person authorized to edit firm-wide appetite YAML; conflating the two roles could actually widen who can touch the rulebook, which cuts against defensibility rather than protecting it (a supervisor asking 'who can change the rules that produced this verdict' wants a narrower answer than 'everyone in 2LoD').
objections.counter_proposal: Gate the YAML editor behind a distinct 'pack author' designation rather than the general 2LoD role — even if, in practice, the same person currently holds both hats. Keep the human-readable lever-cards/citation/jurisdiction-status view open to both 1LoD and 2LoD as AIG-7 and my own F6 already agree on; only the edit/save controls need the narrower gate.

crossExams.revised_position:
I still recommend targeted-redesign, and having read the other five papers I'm more confident in it, not less — every panel independently arrived at 'extend R9, don't rebuild,' from clarity, interaction, layout, governance, and banking-practice angles that don't overlap much with mine. That convergence is itself useful ammunition for the owner: five different professional lenses looked at the same six screens and none of them found a reason to touch the engine, the audit trail, the citation chain, or the honesty markers.

What I concede: my own paper was narrowly focused on the sign-off page and under-weighted two things the other panels caught cleanly — the register list's raw-enum leakage (agreed, no objection) and the internal requirement-tracking IDs (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4) riding along in user-facing prose. I hadn't drawn a sharp line in my own non-negotiables between 'regulatory citation, must stay' and 'internal spec-tracking code, pure noise, should go' — Clarity F5 and Interaction Design ID-1 are right that these are different categories, and I'm adopting that distinction explicitly now rather than leaving it implicit in my citation non-negotiable. I also concede that role-aware defaults (Banking F1, Information Layout's implicit framing) are the right direction for the verdict page's dual-audience problem — 1LoD gets 'what you need to do,' 2LoD gets the full dossier open by default for their own role — provided it's implemented as a default-open-for-the-actual-reviewer, not a permanent collapse that a 2LoD reviewer also has to click through.

What I'm holding the line on, with counter-proposals offered in each case: the sign-off action must not become reachable ahead of the reasoning it depends on (objection to IxD ID-4) — a sticky nav is fine, a sticky Approve button one scroll from the top is not; the 12-rule citation list should compress to one line per rule, not collapse to 1-of-12 by default (objection to Information Layout F3) — Clarity's own three-line disclosure shape, applied here, gets the density win without dropping 11 citations below a fold; 'translation fidelity: unattested' needs a compact but persistent presence on every verdict-bearing screen, not consolidation onto the one screen where it's actionable (objection to Information Layout F7 / IxD ID-7); and decision_type/hitl need to stay out of any 'advanced fields' toggle that platform/vendor might reasonably go behind (objection to IxD ID-3), because F5's whole point is that their silence needs to stay visible, not get easier to produce unnoticed. None of these objections block the redesign — each has a concrete counter-proposal that gets the requesting panel's actual goal (less clutter, faster path to sign-off, cleaner header, simpler form) without cutting the specific disclosure I'm responsible for protecting. My proposed direction is otherwise unchanged: extend R9 to the sign-off page, register list, and policy screen, with the seven items above as the precise seams where 'less technical' and 'still defensible' need to be negotiated in the same PR rather than assumed to be free."

proposal.headline: Six panels, six independent lenses, one verdict: AIGate is not too technical because of what it says — it is too technical because of where and how it says it. Nothing in the engine, the rules, the audit trail, or the honesty markers needs to change. What needs to change is the order, grouping and vocabulary on the four screens that never received the treatment the graph-review screen got in Round 9 — the verdict/sign-off page, the guided intake form, the register list and the appetite-framework screen — plus one screen none of the panels caught: the Confirm & attest step still shows raw codes ("traditional-ml · L3 · Zone B · execute") at the exact moment a submitter signs their name to the description. I recommend a targeted redesign delivered as one coordinated round of five build chunks, in the R9 manner (aggregate, prioritise, put one click away — never delete). Not a copy patch: it would leave the verdict page and the form as confusing as today. Not a full redesign: no panel found a fault in the flow or the information architecture, and a rebuild would put the caveats that make the product defensible first in line to be lost. Every disagreement between panels is settled below by a stated principle rather than a vote, and every overruled position is recorded. Three facts from the code that neither round of the panels had: the sign-off buttons are already hidden from the 1LoD role today (so the role-gating fight was about a decision already shipped — the fix is to label the role switcher honestly), the verdict page already has an accessible fold component with an honesty-floor override (so the recomposition is cheaper than the panels assumed), and the "describe in plain language" path is already the default entry point.
proposal.proposal_markdown:
# AIGate — reconciled design proposal (chair's report)

**Date:** 23 August 2026 · **Build reviewed:** v0.16.0 · **Panels:** Clarity & plain language · Interaction design · Information layout & accessibility · AI governance · Regulation & supervisory defensibility · Banking practice (James 1LoD / Priya 2LoD)

---

## 1. The headline

Your instinct was right: a first-line business person meeting this product today would be confused, and a reviewer would find the verdict page a wall. But every panel, working separately from six different professional angles, reached the same diagnosis: **the confusion comes from presentation, not from substance.** The questions the product asks are the right questions; the verdict says the right things; the honesty markers ("provisional", "unverified", "guessed", "self-asserted name") are the product's spine. The problem is that:

1. Four screens never received the Round-9 treatment (the recomposition that fixed the graph-review screen in August): the **verdict/sign-off page**, the **guided intake form**, the **register list**, and the **appetite-framework screen**.
2. The engine's internal vocabulary leaks through in three specific ways: raw workflow codes (`pre_checked`) in the register; internal requirement-tracking codes (`LC-2`, `NF-2`, `PE-4`, `VD-4`, `UC-4`) inside sentences a bank reviewer reads; and a technical code in brackets after every one of ~90 options on the intake form.
3. One screen nobody on the panels caught (found by the chair in the source): the **Confirm & attest** step, where the submitter clicks "Confirm and evaluate" — the attestation moment — still shows `traditional-ml · L3 · Zone B · execute`.

**Recommendation: targeted redesign** — one coordinated round, five build chunks, method governed by the R9 precedent (aggregate, prioritise, layer; never delete an honesty disclosure). Nothing touches `src/engine`, the audit model, or the three-lever architecture.

Three things the panels argued about that the code already settles (see §6 for how this changes the resolutions):
- The Approve / Request correction / Challenge buttons are **already** rendered only in the 2LoD role (`RegisterDetail.tsx`, `showActionBar = role === '2LoD' && stage === 'pre_checked'`), and the "Rule challenges" menu item is already hidden for 1LoD. The role-gating dispute was about a decision already shipped. What is missing is honesty about what the role switcher *is* — a view preference in a build with no sign-in — not the gating itself.
- The verdict page already has a native, accessible fold component (`<details>`) with an honesty-floor override ("never fold while any control is UNVERIFIED"). The recomposition reuses it; the accessibility cost the Layout panel worried about is close to zero.
- The plain-language "Describe" box is already step 1 for everyone; only the model-based *reading* of it is gated on a local model being configured. No change needed there.

---

## 2. The principles used to settle every conflict

These are the product's own constitution, restated so you can see why each call went the way it did:

| # | Principle | What it means in practice |
|---|---|---|
| **P1 — Honesty is the floor** | No honesty marker or regulatory citation is removed, softened, or moved off the screen where the decision it qualifies is made. The UI never implies a capability it lacks (sign-in, access control, verified evidence). | "Provisional" stays glued to "Approved with controls"; the self-asserted-name caveat stays next to the Approve button; a role switcher that hides controls must say it is a view, not a lock. |
| **P2 — Comprehension is the goal** | The first thing a non-technical reader sees on any element is a plain sentence; the technical term sits beside it or one click away — never the only label, never hidden. | "Personal details of clients" first, `Client PII` small and grey beside it. |
| **P3 — R9 governs method** | Aggregate, prioritise, layer — never delete. One carve-out, stated openly: internal requirement-tracking codes (`LC-2`, `NF-2`…) are engineering exhaust, not disclosures, and are removed outright; the sentence they sat in survives untouched. | The 12-rule list compresses to 12 one-liners; it does not become "1 of 12, click for the rest". |
| **P4 — Both-sides designs beat winners** | Plain word + code; summary then detail; per-role *defaults*, never per-role *locks*. | Form section headers read "What it uses (input data)". |
| **P5 — Accessibility is part of comprehension** | No meaning delivered by hover alone; every new fold/toggle carries programmatic open/closed state. | Tier/Track meanings become an always-visible legend, not a tooltip. |
| **P6 — Reserved words and determinism** | Every new rendered string passes the `/approved|rejected/i` gate; nothing changes in the engine; every change is presentation-only (Rule 4). | Stage label for `approved` becomes "Cleared", not "Approved". |

---

## 3. Per screen — keep / change / redesign (ordered by impact on the two users)

### 3.1 Verdict / sign-off page (register → case detail) — **REDESIGN (recomposition; content unchanged)**

**Who it hurts today:** both users end here. James has to scroll past a full effective-challenge dossier to learn what to do; Priya reads a dense paragraph of rule IDs and citation brackets, and the single thing she most needs first — "this is provisional, here is why" — is the fourth element in reading order.

**What changes (wireframe of the target state, 2LoD view):**

```
← register

Tier: High   Track: II        Approved with controls · Provisional
Not final — 9 controls still to put in place and a second-line sign-off still needed.
High tier = a lot could go wrong if this misbehaves; waits for second-line sign-off.
Track II = overseen as a model with extra scrutiny.

[PROVISIONAL — review required before this is final]            ← moved up to here
 Cause: no country rulebook was applied, so only your firm's own rules were used.

BEFORE YOU SIGN OFF — five things to check        (each line jumps to its section)

 ☐ 9 controls named · 8 outstanding · 1 in place · evidence: 1 verified, 8 unverified → Controls
 ☐ No country rulebook applied — firm rules only. If UK/EU/US applies, say so and re-run → Jurisdiction
 ☐ Rulebook translation: unattested — nobody has yet confirmed the policy wording

[section nav, sticks to top while scrolling, collapses at high zoom]

VERDICT  Approved with controls · Provisional  — Inside appetite once 9 controls are in place…

WHAT YOU NEED TO DO  (summary-then-detail; default collapsed per item, "Expand all")

 … (each ▸ opens: description · "closed by" controls · full citation text)
 Measured against 5 hard lines and 18 firm rules (invariants) — 12 apply and are not yet satisfied.

▸ How fragile is this approval?   (fold, closed — as today)

THE CONTROL SET, WITH EVIDENCE STATUS  (stays unfolded while any control is UNVERIFIED — as today)
▸ What would make this verdict expire (fold, closed — as today)
Risk-knowledge awareness  (visibly different container — dashed; "Informs — the rules decide" kept)
▸ Similar decided cases (collapsed to a count — as today)

SIGN-OFF  (2LoD role only — as today)
 Your name ______  Recorded on the attestation so the trail says who accepted this verdict.
                  It is self-asserted — this build has no sign-in, so the name is not verified.  ← protected, verbatim
```
