
**Specific moves and who asked for them:**
- Provisional banner moves to directly after the title/chip row (Layout F4). The risk-gap sentence gets its advisory qualifier at first mention (Governance AIG-4).
- Status row: plain lead sentence added; the literal pair "Approved with controls · Provisional" stays together beside it (Clarity F2 + Regulation's additive condition); the raw `pre_checked` token leaves this row — the lead sentence says it in words.
- "Before you sign off" checklist header, derived purely from existing state, each line a jump link (Regulation F1, Layout F3/F8, Governance's revised position). It is a *compression* of the reasoning — rule names and citations at summary weight — not a bypass. It renders under the same condition the action bar already renders (2LoD role, stage awaiting sign-off). In the 1LoD role the page leads with "What you need to do", exactly as today.
- Sticky **section navigation**, not a sticky Approve button (IxD ID-4's goal, Regulation/Governance/Banking's objection, Layout's zoom caveat). The Approve control stays after the reasoning.
- The 12-rule block becomes **one line per rule, all visible by default, grouped Critical/High/Medium**, plain name first, rule ID as quiet code, citation as a chip; the description and "closed by" list open per rule (Regulation's counter to Layout F3; Clarity F4; Governance AIG-1's three-kind legend).
- Controls list becomes summary-then-detail: one line each with status chip; the three-line "What it is / Why / What in place" opens per item, "Expand all" available. Status chips (OUTSTANDING / IN PLACE / UNVERIFIED) stay on every line (Governance's clarification of Layout F8: items move to "addressed", they never vanish).
- "18 invariants" → "18 firm rules (invariants)" in the stat line (IxD ID-8, Clarity F7).
- Internal codes `(LC-2)`, `(NF-2)`, `(VD-4 / NF-2)` deleted from sentences; the sentences stay (Clarity F5, IxD ID-1, Governance, Regulation). Rule/control IDs and regulatory citations are **not** internal codes — they stay (see build gate G2).
- "Rulebook translation: unattested" appears as a checklist line here, because this is where it bears on the decision (Regulation, Clarity, Banking objections to removing it from the header).
- Protected strings, verbatim, exempt from any copy-shortening: the self-asserted-name caveat; the memo caption; the "Outstanding means…" sentence; the audit-trail proof-of-concept sentence; "Informs — the rules decide" (Regulation F2/F3, Governance, Banking).

### 3.2 Guided intake form (step 3 on the no-model path) — **CHANGE (restructure presentation; same 16 fields, same values)**

**Who it hurts today:** James, in his first ten minutes: 16 flat questions, a bracketed code after every option (~90 of them), and a full risk-methodology paragraph permanently open under several fields.

**Target state:**

```
Guided intake — answer the questions below. No AI reads your answers; the same answers always give the same outcome.
5 sections · 16 questions (13 required) · about ten minutes

1  ABOUT IT
   What do you want to call it? *        In a sentence or two, what does it do? *

2  WHAT IT USES  (input data)
   What kind of information does it use? *   — Pick the most sensitive kind it touches.   Why we ask ▸
     ○ Public — already published or freely available                    Public
     ○ Everyday business information — nothing sensitive                 Internal
     ○ Personal details of clients — names, accounts, anything identifying them   Client PII
     ○ Price-sensitive information — live deals, unpublished results     MNPI
   Where does that information sit today? *  — Before the AI touches it; if several places, the least protected.  Why we ask ▸

3  WHAT THE AI IS AND HOW IT RUNS  (processing)
   What kind of AI is it? *   How much can it do without a person? *
   Where does the AI itself run? * — Not where the data is stored — where it is sent to be processed.  Why we ask ▸
   Which approved platform does it run on? (optional — blank means: not on an approved platform)
   Whose model or service is it? (optional — blank means: assessed as built in-house)
   Which model does it run on? *

4  WHAT COMES OUT AND WHO IT REACHES  (output)
   What does it actually produce or do? *   Who sees what it produces? *   How much weight does its output carry? *
   If it gets something wrong, can it be undone? *
   What kind of decision does it feed? (optional — leave blank only if it feeds no decision at all)
   Does a person check it before anything happens? (optional)
   How widely is it used? *   ☐ It replaces something we already use

5  WHERE IT APPLIES  (jurisdictions)
   Which countries or regions does it touch? *  ☐ UK ☐ US ☐ EU ☐ CA ☐ SG ☐ JP ☐ None / not sure

One continuous scroll — no Next/Back paging.                                   [Continue]
```

**Specific moves and who asked for them:**
- Five plain-language section headers with the engine term beside each (Layout F6's grouping, IxD's vocabulary objection, Banking's "single scroll, not a wizard" condition). `fieldset`/`legend` for screen readers.
- The bracketed technical term leaves the clickable label and becomes a small, muted, **always-visible** suffix — not a tooltip (Clarity F3, IxD ID-3, Banking F3, Layout's no-hover rule). The code is still there for the model-validation reader; it is no longer what James reads first.
- Help text: one-line prompt always visible; the paragraph behind an accessible "Why we ask" disclosure (Banking F5, mirroring R9-SC-2). Where one extra sentence is load-bearing for a correct answer (e.g. "not where the data is stored — where it is sent to be processed") it stays visible.
- **No field goes behind an "advanced" toggle.** Platform, vendor and model stay visible and first-class (Governance AIG-3 non-negotiable); decision type and human-check stay in the main flow with their "leave blank only if…" guidance (Regulation F5, IxD's Round-2 concession). The "(optional — blank means: …)" phrase makes the meaning of silence explicit on the form itself.

## 6. Options for the owner

**Option A — Patch the copy (1–2 chunks, ~2 days of pipeline work).** `STAGE_LABELS`; strip internal spec codes; technical terms on form options become muted suffixes; "firm rules (invariants)"; no-basis badge reword; Confirm & attest labels; role-switcher honesty label. *Cost:* small; one or two releases; modest test churn. *Risk:* the verdict page stays a wall and the form stays flat — your "too confusing" complaint survives on the two screens that matter most. This is the floor, not the fix.

**Option B — Targeted redesign, one coordinated round (recommended; 5 chunks, roughly 6–9 working days at this project's R9/R14 pace).** Everything in A plus: verdict/sign-off recomposition (§3.1), intake form grouping and help-collapse (§3.2), register default view, grouped chips, legend and banner (§3.3), policy-screen split (§3.4), graph-review refinements and accessibility (§3.6), queue copy (§3.9), header chip (§3.8). Shipped as a requirements round (R-next) with test cases, like R9, so the "never delete" rule is test-enforced. *Cost:* five chunks, each with its own build, three test runs, spec `.md` + `.html` parity, and a live walkthrough; expect to update scoped test queries in several files. *Risk:* moderate and known — reserved-word collisions (gated), an implementer conflating citations with spec IDs (gated by the three-class rule), spec drift (gated by parity check). No engine, audit or honesty change, so the determinism and honesty tests are the safety net.

**Option C — Full redesign (new information architecture / visual language from a fresh mockup; 3–6 weeks plus full re-verification).** *Cost:* high — every disclosure re-derived, `field-copy.ts`/R9/R14 infrastructure discarded, ~540 tests revisited. *Risk:* highest — the hedged-sounding caveats that make the product defensible ("self-asserted", "restates the record; does not strengthen it", "proof-of-concept grade") are the first casualties of a "make it feel finished" pass; and no panel found a fault in the flow that would justify it. Not recommended.

**Recommendation: B.** If you want to see value fastest, build chunk 1 (register) first — it is unanimous, tiny, and a warm-up for the pattern — then the verdict page, then the form.

## 7. Build order and the gates every chunk must pass

**Order (by impact, with the cheapest unanimous item first as a warm-up):**
1. Register list (§3.3) + `STAGE_LABELS` + role-switcher label (§3.8).
2. Verdict / sign-off recomposition (§3.1).
3. Guided intake form (§3.2) + Confirm & attest (§3.5) + questionnaire tag (§3.7).
4. Appetite framework split (§3.4) + header chip (§3.8).
5. Graph review refinements (§3.6) + rule-improvement queue (§3.9).

**Gates (stated once, applied to every chunk):**
- **G1 Reserved words** — every new rendered string checked against `/approved|rejected/i` (verdict status strings excepted).
- **G2 Three classes of code** — spec/requirement IDs deleted; rule/control IDs kept as quiet code beside a plain name; regulatory citations kept as chips. Named in the ticket.
- **G3 Accessibility** — no hover-only meaning; every new fold/toggle has programmatic open/closed state (reuse the native `<details>` Fold; add `aria-expanded` to button toggles); sticky nav collapses at high zoom.
- **G4 Boundaries** — nothing in `src/engine`; presentation-only (Rule 4); determinism test untouched; no new writes from rendering.
- **G5 Protected strings, verbatim** — self-asserted-name caveat; memo caption; "Outstanding means…"; audit-trail proof-of-concept sentence; "Informs — the rules decide"; provisional banner text; "The model proposed everything below…" gate note.
- **G6 Role** — no new conditional rendering by role beyond today's; the switcher says it is a view.
- **G7 House ritual** — `npm test` ×3, `tsc`, build, spec-parity (edit both `.md` and `.html`), live walkthrough of the affected screen, commit and push per milestone.

## 9. Non-negotiables preserved, panel by panel

- **Clarity:** no disclosure removed; canonical vocabulary retrievable on every screen (quiet code / muted suffix); every label has a plain companion via `field-copy.ts`; reserved words gated; R9 shape reused; engine untouched.
- **Interaction design:** deterministic non-chatbot framing and visible "why" kept; each persona's question leads its screen (James: what to do; Priya: before you sign off); internal spec IDs out of prose; reserved words; presentation-only.
- **Information layout & accessibility:** honesty markers by text/icon never colour alone; progressive disclosure never deletes; default-open tracks importance; every disclosure has programmatic state; no raw enum on any screen.
- **AI governance:** proposed/guessed/confident-no-basis per field intact with no-plain-confirm on guessed cards and no "confirm all"; model/vendor/platform first-class; three levers visually distinct with the advisory qualifier at first mention; hard lines / firm rules / country rules kept as three labelled kinds; attestation record intact; no overclaiming.
- **Regulation & supervisory:** every citation stays attached to its rule line; Provisional/UNVERIFIED/OUTSTANDING inseparable from what they qualify; audit trail unfolded, complete, labelled proof-of-concept; named sign-off distinct, with the self-asserted caveat beside Approve; three-lever separation; rule → control → citation → evidence chain traceable end to end.
- **Banking practice:** verdicts traceable to rule and citation even when compressed; honesty markers at full strength; three levers visible; sign-off controls never reachable or visually prominent for the 1LoD view (as today) and the role switcher honest about being a view; plain-language work confined to rendering.

conflicts.resolution: It already is step 1 for everyone; only the model-based reading is gated on a configured local model. No change; one copy check on step 1 for the no-model case.

dissents.dissent: Pin the name/notes/Approve action bar as a sticky element directly under the verdict summary so the trigger lands while motivation is high.
dissents.why_overruled: An attestation control positioned before the evidence it attests to is the ritual-checking failure effective-challenge review exists to prevent (Regulation, Governance, Banking all objected; Layout flagged reflow/focus risk). Their real goal — the reviewer does not hunt for the sign-off — is met by the 'Before you sign off' checklist header and a sticky section nav with a jump link.

dissents.dissent: Fold 'model confident — no verified basis' into the existing 'guessed' visual language.
dissents.why_overruled: Guessed and confident-without-basis are different epistemic states with different gating (guessed cards get no plain confirm); merging their visual language invites merging their logic, which is the automation-bias regression Governance's blocking objection named. The reword for actionability is adopted; the merge is not.

dissents.dissent: Progressively disclose platform, vendor and decision type behind an 'advanced' toggle.
dissents.why_overruled: Model/vendor/platform identity is the data the firm's own silent-substitution rule depends on (Governance non-negotiable) and decision type / human-check are decision-bearing fields whose silence must stay visible (Regulation F5). Density is achieved by grouping and help-collapse instead; no field is hidden.

dissents.dissent: Treat INV-*, CTRL-*, HL-* rule and control IDs as internal identifiers that must never appear in rendered copy.
dissents.why_overruled: Rule and control IDs are the exact audit citation a second-line reviewer needs to map a verdict to the rulebook (Governance, Regulation, Clarity). They stay, demoted to quiet code beside a plain name. Spec/requirement IDs (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4…) are removed, as the panel asked.

dissents.dissent: Remove 'translation fidelity: unattested' from the persistent header, keeping it only where it is actionable.
dissents.why_overruled: It is a pack-level provisional marker that bears on every citation a reviewer weighs at sign-off; removing it from the decision path is a real loss (Clarity, Regulation, Banking). Resolved as compress-to-chip everywhere plus a checklist line on the verdict page — the trunk-test clutter is gone, the disclosure is not.

dissents.dissent: Keep only the single Critical rule and a count visible; fold the full 12-rule list behind 'show all rules'.
dissents.why_overruled: The rule list is the evidentiary chain, not reference material; eleven citations must not sit below a fold by default (Regulation's non-negotiable; Governance and Clarity concurred). The density goal is met by one line per rule with prose behind a per-rule click.

dissents.dissent: Map the approved lifecycle stage to the label 'Approved'.
dissents.why_overruled: It reintroduces the /approved|rejected/i test-fragility trap CLAUDE.md warns about (Clarity's blocking objection) and could overclaim for Low-tier self-service cases; 'Cleared' is used and a shared reserved-word gate applies to all new labels.

dissents.dissent: Render the Approve/Request correction/Challenge block only when the active role is 2LoD, and key the sticky action bar's content to role.
dissents.why_overruled: The first half is already shipped (RegisterDetail.tsx gates the action bar on role and stage in JSX) so it is moot; the second half falls with ID-4. Going further — adding new role-based hiding in a build whose role is a self-selected dropdown — would imply access control that does not exist (Clarity, IxD, Governance). The fix is to label the switcher honestly and make every new role difference a default state.

dissents.dissent: Gate the raw-YAML edit/save control behind the 2LoD role the same way rule challenges already are.
dissents.why_overruled: A case reviewer is not automatically a rule author (Regulation) and a self-asserted role is not a lock (Governance, IxD). Resolved by information-architecture separation — readable rulebook by default, editor behind an explicit disclosure with an honest sentence.

dissents.dissent: Collapse fully-confident quoted fields on the graph review into a one-line 'N fields confirmed automatically' summary per card.
dissents.why_overruled: The values are what the human attests to (R9-SC-2: meaning always visible) and 'confirmed automatically' claims a confirmation that has not happened (Governance non-negotiable). Long quotes may truncate instead.

dissents.dissent: Platform and vendor may go behind progressive disclosure while decision type and human-check stay visible.
dissents.why_overruled: Minor: Governance's non-negotiable that model/vendor/platform remain explicit first-class fields wins; no field is hidden on the guided form.

dissents.panel: Clarity & plain language (F6 mechanism, F2 substitution)
dissents.dissent: Deliver Tier/Track meanings as hover tooltips on the register chips; replace the status chip stack with a plain sentence.
dissents.why_overruled: On mechanism only: hover-only content fails touch, keyboard and screen-reader users (Layout), so the meanings become an always-visible legend; and the literal 'Approved with controls · Provisional' pair must stay beside the new sentence (Regulation). Their content is adopted in full.

dissents.dissent: Reuse GraphView's exact 'Input data / Processing / Output' headings as the form's section headers.
dissents.why_overruled: Modified, not rejected: those are the engine's data-flow words (IxD); the headers read in the submitter's language with the engine term beside them, preserving continuity for the reviewer.

options_for_owner.name: Option A — Patch the copy
options_for_owner.what: STAGE_LABELS for the register; strip internal requirement codes (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4, VD-4, UC-*) from every sentence; technical terms on form options become a small muted suffix; 'firm rules (invariants)'; reword the no-basis badge; plain labels on the Confirm & attest screen; relabel the role switcher as a view preference.
options_for_owner.cost: 1–2 build chunks, roughly two days of pipeline work at the project's R9/R14 pace; one or two releases; modest test churn (scoped queries, reserved-word checks).
options_for_owner.risk: Low technical risk, high product risk: the verdict/sign-off page stays a wall and the intake form stays a flat list of 16 questions, so the 'too confusing' complaint survives on the two screens that matter most. This is the floor, not the fix.

options_for_owner.name: Option B — Targeted redesign, one coordinated round (recommended)
options_for_owner.what: Everything in A plus: verdict/sign-off page recomposed (provisional banner first, 'Before you sign off' checklist with jump links, one line per rule with all citations visible, controls as summary-then-detail, section nav, advisory qualifier at first mention); guided form grouped into five plain-language sections with help behind 'Why we ask' and no field hidden; register with a 2LoD 'awaiting your sign-off' default, grouped filters, an always-visible legend, a provisional banner and a Flags column; appetite-framework screen with the readable rulebook by default and the YAML editor behind a disclosure; graph-review label reuse, badge reword, 'not stated' flag and aria state; queue copy and source tags; header fidelity chip. Shipped as a requirements round with test cases so 'never delete' is test-enforced.
options_for_owner.cost: Five build chunks in order (register → verdict → form + confirm → policy + header → graph review + queue), roughly 6–9 working days at the project's recent pace; each chunk carries the house ritual (tests ×3, typecheck, build, spec .md + .html parity, live walkthrough, commit and push). Expect to update scoped test queries in several files and to write an R-next requirements document first.
options_for_owner.risk: Moderate and known: reserved-word collisions (gated per label), an implementer conflating regulatory citations with spec IDs (gated by the three-class rule), spec drift between .md and .html (parity check), and the Low-tier stage-label semantics needing a builder check before landing. No engine, audit or honesty change, so the determinism and honesty test suites remain the safety net.

options_for_owner.name: Option C — Full redesign
options_for_owner.what: New information architecture and visual language from a fresh mockup; re-derive every screen and every disclosure.
options_for_owner.cost: 3–6 weeks plus full re-verification of ~540 tests; discards field-copy.ts, the R9 and R14 recompositions and the accessible fold infrastructure that already work where applied.
options_for_owner.risk: Highest. The hedged-sounding caveats that make the product defensible — 'self-asserted, not verified', 'restates the record; it does not strengthen it', 'proof-of-concept grade' — are the first casualties of a 'make it feel finished' pass; and no panel found a fault in the flow or architecture that would justify it. Not recommended.

non_negotiables_preserved: Clarity & plain language: no honesty disclosure deleted (unsigned packs stay provisional, controls without evidence stay UNVERIFIED, the audit trail keeps saying client-side / proof-of-concept); canonical vocabulary (enum values, rule IDs, control IDs) stays retrievable on every screen as quiet code or muted suffix while never being the first thing a non-technical reader sees; every new label has a plain-English companion sourced from field-copy.ts (STAGE_LABELS, TIER/TRACK meanings); reserved-word discipline gated on every new string; R9's disclosure shape reused rather than reinvented; determinism and engine untouched (Rule 4 presentation-only).

Interaction design: the deterministic, non-chatbot framing and the plain-English 'why' stay visible; each persona's question leads its screen (James: 'What you need to do'; Priya: 'Before you sign off'); internal spec/requirement IDs (LC-2, NF-2, PE-4, VD-4, UC-*) removed from all rendered prose (rule/control IDs retained as quiet code — recorded dissent); reserved words not reintroduced; the guided-form restructure changes presentation only, never the canonical field set or values.

Information layout & accessibility: every honesty marker (PROVISIONAL, UNVERIFIED, OUTSTANDING, guessed, no-verified-basis) legible by text or icon, never colour alone; progressive disclosure reorders or folds but never deletes; default-open state tracks importance (provisional banner first, evidence table unfolded while anything is unverified); every new fold/toggle carries aria-expanded/aria-controls or uses the native details Fold; no raw enum on any screen; no hover-only meaning (including fixing the header's existing title tooltip).

AI governance: per-field AI-proposed / quoted / guessed / confident-no-basis marking stays intact and the guessed-card no-plain-confirm rule is untouched, with no 'confirm all'; model, vendor and platform remain explicit, correctable, first-class fields on the form and the review; the three-lever split (appetite decides / regulation decides where it applies / knowledge informs) stays visually and structurally distinct with the advisory qualifier attached at first mention; hard lines, firm invariants and jurisdiction-pack rules remain three labelled kinds with a legend, never merged; the attestation record ('Confirmed by you', who proposed vs corrected, provisional-until-signed-off) stays intact; no copy claims more certainty than the system has.

Regulation & supervisory defensibility: every rule line keeps its exact regulatory citation, visible without a click; 'Approved with controls' never renders apart from its 'Provisional' qualifier; the audit trail stays append-only, unfolded, complete and labelled proof-of-concept; named human sign-off stays a distinct action with the self-asserted-identity caveat verbatim beside Approve; the effective-challenge memo keeps 'It restates the record; it does not strengthen it' verbatim; the three-lever separation is visible on every rule-bearing screen (risk-knowledge in a visibly different container); the rule → control → citation → evidence-status chain stays traceable end to end; 'translation fidelity: unattested' stays on the decision path as a chip and a checklist line.

Banking practice & the two users: every verdict stays traceable to a named rule and citation even when compressed for James; Provisional / UNVERIFIED / guessed / no-verified-basis keep their current strength; the three-lever ownership model stays explicit on every rule-bearing screen; sign-off actions remain unreachable and visually absent in the 1LoD view (as already shipped) with the role switcher honestly labelled a view preference; plain-language simplification stays strictly a rendering concern and never reduces the question set, field coverage, or citation depth.

skeptics.lens: Honesty-and-defensibility skeptic: does any element hide/soften a PROVISIONAL/UNVERIFIED/overdue marker, a citation, a named sign-off, the advisory-vs-deciding split, the human-confirmation gate, or the append-only trail — or create audit theatre / raise automation-bias risk?
skeptics.summary: The proposal's core recommendation is sound and unusually well-grounded in the actual source — every claim I spot-checked against GraphView.tsx, ConfirmationStep.tsx, RegisterDetail.tsx, register.ts and field-copy.ts held up, including the two novel code-level facts (role gating already shipped; UC-6 raw codes at attestation). But the fix for that very raw-code defect is scoped to the wrong surface: the same graphSummaryRows() function that produces "traditional-ml · L3 · Zone B · execute" also renders inside VerdictDisplay.tsx's Record & provenance panel on the verdict/sign-off page — the exact page §3.1 is redesigning for Priya — and no part of §3.1 or §3.5 names or fixes that second call site, so a 2LoD reviewer would still meet raw codes at sign-off after the round ships. Separately, the new "Before you sign off" checklist plus a sticky nav item that jumps straight to Sign-off lets a reviewer reach Approve in one click without ever touching the reasoning or evidence — reintroducing, under a different name, the exact ritual-checking risk the chair explicitly rejected ID-4's sticky Approve bar for — and the audit trail's actor field is the same self-asserted, ungated role string that drives whether the Approve button even renders, yet only the signer's name gets an honesty caveat, not the role. Recommend: fix the graph-summary scope gap and the nav/checklist rubber-stamp path before the R-next ticket is written; both are small, targeted amendments that don't touch the recommendation itself.

refutations.problem: graph-summary.ts's graphSummaryRows() — which produces the raw 'traditional-ml · L3 · Zone B · execute' string the chair singles out as the one defect no panel caught — is imported and rendered in TWO places: ConfirmationStep.tsx (which §3.5 explicitly fixes) AND VerdictDisplay.tsx line ~1123, inside the 'Record & provenance' panel on the verdict/sign-off page itself (confirmed by reading both files: `import { graphSummaryRows } from './graph-summary'` in VerdictDisplay.tsx, then `{graphSummaryRows(graph).map(...)}` rendering the same confirmation__grid). §3.1's target-state wireframe lists sections 'Verdict · What the submitter must do · Why · Controls & evidence · Risk knowledge · Sign-off' with no 'Record & provenance' entry, and none of §3.1's 'specific moves' mention it. So after chunk 2 (verdict recomposition) and chunk 3 (Confirm & attest fix) both ship, Priya still meets raw enum codes on the page she signs against — the same class of defect the proposal claims unique credit for catching, left half-fixed by its own scoping.
refutations.fix: Route graphSummaryRows()'s output through field-copy.ts at the shared function (or a shared rendering wrapper used by both callers) rather than fixing ConfirmationStep.tsx in isolation, so VerdictDisplay.tsx's Record & provenance panel gets the same plain-word-first treatment. Add an explicit line item for this panel to §3.1's 'specific moves' list. While in there, also translate the Input-data (data_class) row — §3.5's four worked examples (Model, Autonomy, Data zone, Output) conspicuously omit it even though the same function renders `${input.label} · ${input.data_class}` raw.

refutations.target: §3.1 verdict page — 'Before you sign off' checklist + sticky section nav
refutations.problem: The sticky section nav includes 'Sign-off' as an always-clickable item from the moment the page loads, and the checklist above it is presented as a compressed five-line summary. A 2LoD reviewer can click the nav's Sign-off link within seconds of arrival, entering a name and clicking Approve without ever visiting Why/Controls/Risk-knowledge — the identical shortcut the chair explicitly rejected when overruling IxD's sticky Approve bar ('an attestation control positioned before the evidence it attests to is the ritual-checking failure effective-challenge review exists to prevent'). The checklist's own jump-links to sections a reviewer may never open create a 'looks like due diligence, may not be' surface — audit theatre risk — with no mechanism (view-gating, a soft 'reviewed' affirmation, or simply omitting Sign-off from the always-available nav) proposed to close the gap the proposal itself just argued matters. The product already has a precedent for exactly this kind of gating: ADR-IF-R6-2 renders no plain confirm button on a graph-review card with guessed fields until the human actually opens the editor (confirmed in GraphView.tsx) — that pattern is not reused here.
refutations.fix: Either omit 'Sign-off' from the sticky nav (require scrolling through the reasoning, as today, to reach it) or gate the Approve control's enabled state behind having expanded/visited the checklist items at least once, mirroring ADR-IF-R6-2's precedent that a confirm action can be legitimately withheld until the human has actually looked.

refutations.target: §3.8 role-switcher relabel ('Viewing as — a view preference; this build has no sign-in')
refutations.problem: RegisterDetail.tsx confirms the entire action bar (Approve/Request correction/Challenge) is gated purely on the client-side string `role === '2LoD'` (line 548), and every audit event this round writes records `actor: role` — the same unauthenticated, self-selected string (lines 245, 283, 415, 451, 506). The proposal correctly makes the role switcher honestly say it's not a permission, but that honesty is one-sided: the signer's *name* field already carries a caveat ('self-asserted... not verified') displayed right beside Approve, while the *role* that determined whether Approve was even reachable — and that gets written into every audit event as `actor` — carries no equivalent caveat anywhere in the redesign, including on the audit-trail display itself (§9's non-negotiables list preserves 'named sign-off distinct... with the self-asserted caveat beside Approve' but says nothing about the role dimension).
refutations.fix: Add the same 'self-asserted, no sign-in' caveat next to the role indicator on the sign-off block (not just the header switcher), and render the audit-trail's actor field with that caveat attached wherever a 2LoD-gated event (approve, request-correction, challenge) is displayed — so a later reader of the trail cannot over-trust `actor: 2LoD` as more verified than the name field beside it.

refutations.target: §3.3 register — Stage label 'Cleared' for the 'approved' lifecycle stage
refutations.problem: register.ts / workflow-router.ts confirm the same lifecycle stage value `approved` is reached by two different provenance paths: a Low-tier case that never had a human reviewer touch it ('self-service' in workflow-router.ts, TC-LC-2-01) and a Critical/High/Medium-tier case that reached it only via handleApprove() — an actual 2LoD reviewer clicking Approve (register.ts line 424, `updateLifecycleStage(useCaseId, 'approved', role)`). 'Cleared' is a single, passive, actor-free word applied to both, flattening exactly the distinction — was this actually signed off by a named human, or did it just clear the bar untouched — that is the product's core differentiator. The chair's own text flags this as unresolved ('*Builder check:* confirm the two labels against the Low-tier lifecycle before they land') yet still recommends shipping the label.
refutations.fix: Resolve before the ticket is written rather than leaving it as an open builder check: either keep 'Cleared' but rely explicitly on the adjacent Tier column to carry the self-service/reviewed distinction (state that reliance in writing), or use two labels distinguished by provenance so the Stage column alone still answers 'was this human-approved.'

skeptics.lens: Feasibility for James (1LoD, 10 min) and Priya (2LoD, queue of 12), checked against the actual v0.16.0 codebase, the requirements history (R9 through R14), and the engine-island/determinism/audit constraints — verifying every "fact from the code" the chair claims, not just the argument structure.
skeptics.summary: The core call — targeted redesign, presentation-only, five chunks in the R9 manner — is sound and every constraint that matters (engine island, determinism, append-only audit, honesty markers) is genuinely respected; most of the chair's "facts from the code" check out under direct inspection. But the headline claim that the verdict/sign-off page "never received the Round-9 treatment" is factually wrong — requirements-014.md shows an R14 recomposition applying that exact idiom (folds, honesty-floor-never-folds, "What you need to do" moved under the headline) was approved and shipped in the same v0.16.0 build the chair reviewed, which both inflates chunk 2's portrayed scope/cost and undercuts the document's central "we found what the panels couldn't see" claim. Five further concrete gaps — a shared raw-code-rendering function split across two build chunks, a checklist that visually promises interactivity it doesn't have, a register column change that contradicts an existing Must-level test/spec requirement without a planned requirements amendment, an under-flagged collision with the codebase's known brittle `/approved|rejected/i` test pattern on the exact page being rewritten, and one internally contradictory build gate — need fixing before a build session should start, but none of them touch the recommendation itself: this survives as Option B once those six items are corrected in the document.

refutations.target: Headline / §1 and §3.1 — "the verdict/sign-off page ... never received the Round-9 treatment"
refutations.problem: Factually false. requirements/requirements-014.md records Round 14, "The Verdict Screen Recomposed," approved 2026-08-18 and explicitly scoped as "the R9 idiom applied to the verdict screen" — folds with data-carrying gist lines, an honesty-floor-never-folds rule, "What you need to do" moved directly under the headline before tier/track, sentence-case copy cleanup. Its changelog says "built and shipped in v0.16.0 (659 tests)" — the exact build the chair's own document header cites as reviewed. The evidence transcript the proposal itself quotes (closed folds "How fragile is this approval?", "Platform & vendor inheritance", "What would make this verdict expire"; "What you need to do" already positioned first) is R14's shipped output, not an unrecomposed screen. This means: (a) the "three facts from the code neither panel had" boast missed a fourth, more central fact sitting in the same requirements/ directory the proposal cites by name for R9; (b) chunk 2's true remaining scope is materially smaller than portrayed — it's refinement of an already-recomposed screen, closer in kind to §3.6's "KEEP; four small changes" than to a first-pass redesign; (c) the 6-9 day Option B estimate is inflated accordingly.
refutations.fix: Correct the headline and §3.1 framing to "received R14, a partial R9-idiom pass, on 2026-08-18 — this round finishes the job": list exactly what R14 already delivered (fold structure, ordering, honesty floor) versus what's still missing (provisional-banner position, raw pre_checked chip, internal spec codes in prose, 12-rule compression, controls summary-then-detail, the sign-off checklist, translation-fidelity checklist line). Re-cost chunk 2 against the smaller residual scope.

refutations.target: §3.5 Confirm & attest vs. VerdictDisplay.tsx "What you told us" fold
refutations.problem: graph-summary.ts's graphSummaryRows() is shared between ConfirmationStep.tsx (the screen the proposal fixes) and VerdictDisplay.tsx's "What you told us" fold, which renders the identical raw codes (traditional-ml, L3, Zone B, execute) on the verdict page itself — the page Priya reads before she signs. Neither the proposal's headline ("one screen none of the panels caught") nor the §3.1 wireframe mentions this second consumer at all; the wireframe's fold sequence omits "What you told us" entirely. The build order (§7) puts the verdict recomposition in chunk 2 and the Confirm & attest fix in chunk 3 — so for at least one release, chunk 2 will ship a "recomposed" verdict page whose declared-values fold still shows the exact raw codes the chair calls out as the product's worst remaining honesty-adjacent gap.
refutations.fix: Note graph-summary.ts as a shared dependency in §3.1 and §3.5, move the graphSummaryRows() label fix into chunk 2 (or make chunk 2 explicitly depend on it), and add "What you told us" to the §3.1 wireframe so a builder doesn't miss it.

refutations.target: §3.1 "Before you sign off" checklist — the ☐ glyphs
refutations.problem: The checklist renders five items with a ☐ prefix and says each "jumps to its section" — i.e., they are static facts with a jump-link, not completable tasks. But ☐ means a real, togglable checkbox input everywhere else in this exact product, including elsewhere in this same proposal: §3.2's guided-form wireframe uses ☐ for the actual "It replaces something we already use" checkbox and the actual UK/US/EU/CA/SG/JP jurisdiction checkboxes, a few sections away in the same document. A non-technical reviewer (the persona this whole redesign is for) encountering ☐ on the sign-off checklist has every reason, from the product's own established vocabulary, to expect it can be ticked and will disappear when handled — which it can't and won't. That is precisely the interaction-design confusion the redesign exists to eliminate, reintroduced by the redesign's own notation.
refutations.fix: Use a distinct glyph/affordance for the read-and-jump checklist (e.g. a chevron or bullet, not a checkbox square) so it's visually distinguishable from the product's real checkbox inputs, and say so explicitly in gate G3 alongside the fold/toggle accessibility rule.

refutations.target: §3.3 Register "Flags" column vs. RegisterView.test.tsx TC-RG-2-02 / register-lifecycle.md §10.2
refutations.problem: An existing Must-level acceptance test (TC-RG-2-02, "2LoD view shows all use cases ... with the §10.2 column set including Submitter and Stale") asserts a named "Stale" column/badge (.register-view__stale-badge) sourced from a formal requirements document, register-lifecycle.md §10.2. The proposal's §3.3 collapses Stale and Sampling into a single "Flags" column as if it were a pure presentation tweak, gated only by the generic G7 test ritual — it never flags that this changes a documented Must fit-criterion and would, under this project's own GVM discipline (every other change in this document is careful to cite the requirement or ADR it touches), need a requirements amendment before or alongside the build chunk, not just an updated test query.
refutations.fix: Either drop the Stale/Sampling merge from scope, or add an explicit requirements-amendment step to chunk 1 that updates register-lifecycle.md §10.2's column-set requirement and re-derives TC-RG-2-02 before the code changes, consistent with how the rest of the document treats requirement-level changes.

refutations.target: Gate G1 vs. WalkingSkeleton.test.tsx:95/157 and VerdictDisplay.inheritance.test.tsx:33
refutations.problem: CLAUDE.md's own gotcha, which this document quotes as a governing principle, names a real single-match `getByText(/approved|rejected/i)` failure mode. Grep confirms exactly this query exists today, unscoped, on the verdict/sign-off page — precisely the screen §3.1 adds the most new copy to (a checklist rendered directly beside the existing "Approved with controls · Provisional" chip stack the proposal deliberately keeps intact). G1 states the rule generically ("every new rendered string checked") but never names these two specific pre-existing brittle test call sites as the highest-probability collision point of the entire round, despite the chair having clearly read the CLAUDE.md passage closely enough to quote it.
refutations.fix: Name WalkingSkeleton.test.tsx:95/157 and VerdictDisplay.inheritance.test.tsx:33 explicitly in chunk 2's ticket as "scope these queries before adding checklist copy," not just a generic reserved-word gate.

refutations.target: Gate G6 vs. §3.3's new 2LoD default "awaiting your sign-off (N)" view
refutations.problem: G6 states "no new conditional rendering by role beyond today's; the switcher says it is a view." But §3.3 explicitly proposes a new role-conditional default: today RegisterView.tsx shows 2LoD all rows unfiltered (`if (!is2LoD) return rows`, no default stageFilter); the proposal adds a new default scoping to pending-sign-off rows for the 2LoD role specifically. That is new conditional behavior keyed to role, which G6 as literally worded forbids. The intent is clearly to freeze access-control-flavored gating (sign-off buttons, the YAML editor), not UI convenience defaults, but the gate doesn't say so, leaving it able to be read either as blocking the register default-view feature the proposal itself wants, or as license to add other role-keyed defaults elsewhere that the document didn't intend.
refutations.fix: Reword G6 to distinguish "no new role-gated access to controls or data" (frozen) from "role-scoped default views/conveniences are fine" (allowed), and cite §3.3 as the worked example.

refutations.target: Conflict #3 resolution (no sticky Approve bar) vs. the brief's own "Priya, queue of 12" framing
refutations.problem: The resolution is principled (attestation must follow the evidence it attests to) and I don't think it's wrong, but it's argued purely on defensibility grounds without weighing it against the throughput need the chair's own opening paragraph names as one of the two things this redesign must serve. A sticky section nav still requires Priya to scroll back to the bottom of a page with 12 visible rule lines, a controls table and a risk-knowledge panel to reach Approve, on every one of her 12 queued cases — the jump links help her get to information, not get out to sign-off faster once she's satisfied. That may be the right trade-off, but the document doesn't show the trade-off was actually made against the stated persona constraint, only against the other panels' objections.
refutations.fix: Add one sentence to the conflict-3 resolution acknowledging the throughput cost for a queue of 12 and why defensibility wins anyway (e.g., "a reviewer who signs 12 cases in the time it takes to scroll past what they're signing is the automation-bias failure the audit trail exists to catch") — makes the trade-off explicit rather than implicit.
